Overlord’s Solana blockchain C2 URL hosting

The RAT implements a resilient C2 server discovery mechanism by using the Solana blockchain. The actor embeds encrypted C2 URLs into the Solana blockchain using the Solana Memo Program, a native Solana program that validates and permanently records arbitrary text strings in the blockchain ledger as part of a transaction. Any Solana wallet can include a memo instruction in a transaction of up to 566 bytes of arbitrary data to the permanent, globally replicated transaction record.

Figure 8. The Snippet of Overlord RAT function queries the Solana Memo address.

A threat actor can post one such transaction from a controlled wallet address whenever the C2 server address needs to be updated. Every deployed RAT picks up the update on its next discovery cycle without any redeployment or reconfiguration.

This is achieved by first retrieving the transaction history for the actor-controlled wallet using the Solana getSignatures JSON-RPC method which receives a chronologically ordered list of transaction signatures with the newest transaction first. For each signature it fetches the full transaction via getTransaction with jsonParsed encoding, which instructs the RPC node to decode every instruction data field into structured JSON response. The RAT module then walks every instruction in the parsed transaction looking for one whose data string is exactly 43 characters in length. The 43-character length is the fixed string length produced when a Base58-encoded WebSocket URL is AES-256 encrypted. Any instruction whose data field is a different length will be skipped, including legitimate Memo transactions from other users and all other Solana program instructions. Only instructions matching this precise length signature are treated as C2 memos.

Figure 9. RPC response format for the getTransaction request.

Good Game stealer

The Good Game stealer payload Talos observed in the arsenal of UAT-12643 is a publicly available Python-based infostealer developed under the label "Good Game (version 1.1.2)” by CirqueiraDev. The actor of this campaign is not the developer, and the malware is distributed as a self-contained Windows executable produced by packaging a Python 3.12.0 code with PyInstaller. Its architecture is split between two cooperating bytecode modules. The “final_build.pyc” acts as the launcher, decoy interface, and reverse-shell client, while “kora.pyc” contains the full data-harvesting stealer logic.

Good Game’s anti-analysis and evasion

The malware employs evasion techniques at every stage of execution, beginning the moment the process starts. The launcher immediately retrieves the console window handle via GetConsoleWindow() and calls ShowWindow() to hide the terminal window. A fully functional Notepad-style graphical user interface (GUI) is rendered in the foreground via tkinter, a Python’s standard, built-in library used for creating GUIs while all malicious threads run as daemon threads behind it.

Before the stealer module begins with any data collection, it runs three sequential execution checks. First, it confirms the host operating system is Windows by checking platform.system(); the stealer aborts silently on Linux or macOS. Second, it verifies network connectivity by performing an HTTP GET request to Google, and if the request fails, the stealer exits and records the failure reason in a file named “skipped" in the temporary directory. Third, and most significantly, it runs sandbox detection checks in five steps.

It checks for the presence of libraries including sbiedll.dll, api_log.dll, vmcheck.dll, wpespy.dll, cmdvrt64.dll, avghookx.dll, snxhk.dll, and guard32.dll.

The MAC address check extracts the host's network adapter hardware address via the getmac module and compares it against known OUI prefixes assigned to virtualization vendors: VMware (00:05:69, 00:0c:29, 00:50:56), VirtualBox (08:00:27), Hyper-V (00:15:5d), Xen (00:16:3e), and Parallels (00:1c:42).

The hardware memory check queries GlobalMemoryStatusEx through a ctypes MEMORYSTATUS structure and flags machines with less than two gigabytes of physical RAM as sandbox environments.

The boot-time check uses psutil.boot_time() to compute system uptime and treats an uptime of fewer than five minutes as indicative of a freshly provisioned analysis VM.

Finally, the Wine emulation check probes for the presence of “C:\windows\system32\wineboot.exe” to detect Windows API compatibility layers.

If any single check triggers, the stealer exits silently, leaving no harvested data and minimal trace.

The decoy URL mechanism of the stealer adds a further layer of camouflage. It opens a PDF-hosted document in the victim's default browser exactly once per machine and computes an MD5 hash of the URL and stores a flag file named “url_opened_<hash>.flag” in the temporary directory of the victim machine. On all subsequent executions, the lure URL is not re-opened, preventing repeated suspicious browser launches that would alert the victim.

Figure 10. Decoy PDF opened by Good Game stealer in victim’s browser.

Persistence established by Good Game

The malware establishes persistence through two independent mechanisms on Windows, ensuring the implant survives reboots regardless of which pathway is disrupted. The primary method is a registry autorun by opening the key HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run using winreg.KEY_SET_VALUE” and writes the absolute filesystem path of the running executable under the value name Zoipers, causing the binary to be launched automatically at every subsequent user logon without requiring elevated privileges. The secondary persistence mechanism is executed from within the stealer module of kora.pyc. The stealer copies the running executable into the Windows Startup folder at %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\ using shutil.copy().

Beyond simple re-execution persistence, the stealer also temporarily disables the Windows Task Manager during its active operation. It calls advapi32.RegCreateKeyExW directly through ctypes against the key HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System and sets a DWORD value DisableTaskMgr=1 via RegSetValueExW. After the data exfiltration completes successfully, the stealer restores the value to zero (DisableTaskMgr=0), reducing the probability that the victim will notice the restriction.

Good Game stealer functionalities

The stealer's most extensive capability targets 23 Chromium-family and Firefox-based browser variants, covering Google Chrome across all distribution channels, Microsoft Edge, Opera, Opera GX, Brave, Vivaldi, Yandex Browser and all its regional variants, Amigo, Torch, Kometa, Orbitum, CentBrowser, 7Star, Sputnik, Epic Privacy Browser, Uran, and Iridium.

The stealer scans LevelDB stores across Discord clients and over 19 Chromium-based browsers for authentication tokens using two regex patterns one for plain-text tokens and one for tokens encrypted with the “dQw4w9WgXcQ:” prefix introduced in newer Discord versions. It decrypts the stolen token via the browser's extracted master key, then validates each recovered token against the Discord API to build a complete account profile covering username, display name, user ID, email, phone number, Nitro subscription tier, linked payment methods, gift codes, and multi-factor authentication (MFA) status.

The stealer additionally extracts ROBLOSECURITY cookies from browser databases, validating each against the Roblox authentication API to confirm active sessions and retrieve the associated account details. A full system profile is assembled covering hostname, username, hardware specifications, OS details, network interfaces, and public IP geolocation metadata queried from ipwhois.app, serialized to system_infos.txt in the archive root.

The stealer also captures a full-monitor screenshot and a single webcam frame, both saved as PNGs and added to the archive before the temporary files are deleted and terminated. The stealer then harvests session data from 21 cryptocurrency wallets including Exodus, Electrum, Ledger Live, Trezor Suite, Atomic Wallet, Trust Wallet, Coinbase, and Binance, as well as four gaming platform launchers (Steam, Riot Games, Epic Games, and Rockstar Games).

Beyond structured credential databases, the stealer conducts a targeted sweep of the victim's personal file system across the folders Desktop, Downloads, Documents, Pictures, Videos, OneDrive root, and the Windows Recent Items folder at %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Recent. The sweep applies to two independent filters that a file must satisfy simultaneously before it is collected.

The first filter is an extension allowlist covering 45 file types spanning different categories mentioned in the table below:

The second filter is a keyword allowlist of four languages English, French, Spanish, and Portuguese that must match the file's base name exactly. The keyword list is designed to maximize overlap with the types of sensitive documents that cryptocurrency users, online gamers, and financially active individuals are likely to store on their desktops or in their documents folders. It covers two-factor authentication backup codes, mnemonic seed phrases, cryptocurrency wallet application names, generic password file naming conventions, banking and payment terms, private key and recovery phrase labels, Discord authentication tokens, Telegram session identifiers, and generic high-value labels such as secret, vault, backup, admin, and root.

Files that satisfy both the extension and keyword filters are written into the archive in the temporary directory, with each file name suffixed by a randomly generated four-digit number before the extension.

Figure 11. Targeted files search and exfiltration program for Good Game stealer.

Data exfiltration mechanism of Good Game stealer

All harvested data is written progressively into a single ZIP file. The ZIP file object is opened with ZIP_DEFLATED compression in the system temporary directory. The archive file name uses the prefix “SK_”, followed by eight randomly generated characters, creating a unique identifier per victim and making the archive harder to identify by name alone.

The ZIP is structured into named subdirectories such as Screenshot/, Webcam/, Session Files/Wallets/, Session Files/Game Launchers/, Session Files/Apps/Telegram/, and Interesting Files/ alongside flat files in the root for system information and antivirus enumeration results. Browser-derived outputs are labelled with a count suffix such as Passwords (N).txt, where N reflects the number of credentials recovered from that browser, enabling the actor to prioritize.

Once all stealer modules have been completed, the closed archive is uploaded to hxxps[:]//upload[.]gofile[.]io/uploadFile using an HTTP POST request. The server returns a JSON response containing a direct download link to the uploaded archive.

Figure 12. Snippet of Good Game stealer exfiltration function.

With the GoFile download URL in hand, the stealer constructs a Discord webhook notification and POSTs it to the hardcoded webhook endpoint. The notification takes the form of a Discord message containing the victim's hostname, username, machine architecture, operating system version, and OS release label providing the operator with an immediate preview of the victim's machine profile without needing to download the archive first. After the webhook POST completes, the stealer calls its cleanup routine to delete the local ZIP archive and all temporary intermediate files including the screenshot PNG and webcam PNG from the temporary directory.

Figure 13. Snippet of Good Game that POSTs reconnaissance data to Discord Webhook.

Clipboard hijacker targets multi-cryptocurrency wallet addresses

The clipboard hijacker Talos identified in the actor’s toolset is a compact Windows x64 executable written in C++. It has no network component or C2 communication protocol; instead, the actor configuration is compiled directly into the binary as XOR-encrypted wallet addresses in the binary data section.

Upon execution, the binary dynamically resolves the API function addresses and creates a global mutex “UuuRjinBZPBMIjnc”. Then it retrieves the machine name and searches for the substrings including VBOX, VMWARE, QEMU, and SANDBOX. Persistence is established by copying the binary to %APPDATA%\MsgEdgeUpdate.exe with FILE_ATTRIBUTE_HIDDEN and FILE_ATTRIBUTE_SYSTEM attributes applied, then adding it under user hive’s Run registry key with value named “MsgEdgeUpdate”, spoofing the appearance of a legitimate Microsoft Edge updater process.

The hijacker polls the Windows clipboard every 500 milliseconds in an infinite loop, applying address-format fingerprinting to detect the copied cryptocurrency. All clipboard APIs are resolved dynamically through user32.dll. On detection, the corresponding attacker wallet address is XOR-decrypted from the data section and overwrites the original wallet address in the victim machine clipboard.

Title: Who was that trying to phone me just now? How one-ring phone scams work
Context: It may feature an international dialling code or be spoofed to appear as a local number
Full Text:
Scammers are past masters at using our humanity against us. That’s why they deploy social engineering tactics like urgency or FOMO to rush us into poor decision making. And it’s why they weaponize our innate curiosity to make their one-ring (“wangiri”) scams work so well.

Wangiri fraud is happening increasingly frequently. Nearly half (45%) of global carriers polled by the Global Leaders' Forum (GLF) last year said they’d experienced a high volume of this type of scam, up from 38% in 2021. The percentage reporting a high financial impact increased from 21% to 32% over the same period.

If the phone rang once and abruptly stopped, would you be tempted to call it back? There are a growing number of reasons to stop and think before you do so.

How do one-ring scams work?

Wangiri is a Japanese term that’s a combination of the words “one ring” and “cut.” The scams combine number spoofing, spamming and international revenue share fraud (IRSF) to part you with your money. The scam itself is disarmingly simple:

You receive a phone call from an unfamiliar number. It may feature an international dialling code or be spoofed to appear as a local number. It rings once before the caller hangs up abruptly, leaving no message.

Perhaps you were waiting for an important call for work, or are simply curious to know who it was. Either way, your curiosity is piqued so you call back.

The call connects to a premium-rate international number which immediately starts costing your money. You might be kept on the line with an automated message, potentially explaining how you could win a prize or receive an important delivery.

The scammers receive a share of the profits generated by the premium number.

The extra money you end up paying, some of which will find its way into the pocket of the fraudster, comes from the premium-rate number and the fact it is likely to be an international call. For the scammers, automated software makes it easy to make these spam calls in large volumes at a relatively low cost. That means they only need a small percentage of recipients to fall for the scam to make it worth their while.

According to the GLF, the top two most targeted countries globally are the US and UK.

Are international numbers always suspicious?

Not all calls from abroad should be treated with suspicion. You might receive legitimate incoming calls and messages from hotels and other businesses based overseas, or even local companies that use call centers abroad. The key is to spot the combination of warning signs: an unfamiliar number, an abrupt end to the connection, and potentially a string of similar calls coming in from different numbers.

Bear in mind too that Calling Line Identification (CLI) or Caller ID spoofing is relatively easier for fraudsters to achieve today. This will enable them to show their international call as coming from a local number, which could persuade you to call back.

Are wangiri calls getting more popular?

One-call scams have been around for years. The FCC issued a warning about them as far back as 2019. But they appear to be growing in popularity. That’s because campaigns are relatively cheap and easy to operate, generating a decent RoI even if only a small number of victims call back. They can also be difficult for carriers to trace and block, given that international calls are often routed via various third parties. And if one number does get blocked, it’s simple for the fraudster to move onto another.

To make their scam more convincing, fraudsters could follow up with a text message, using that old social engineering tactic of creating urgency to persuade you to call back. It could be something good (a time-limited offer or prize) or something bad (a fine or threat if you don’t call back). There are also reports that scammers are targeting businesses to generate automated callbacks, making them even more money before a human notices what’s happening.

How can I stay safe from missed call scams?

Operators are doing their best to improve validation of traffic and spot unusual call patterns, using AI-powered analytics. But sufficient international collaboration is still often lacking at a scale that could make a real impact on spam call volumes. That puts the onus on you to protect yourself from one-ring phone scams.

Consider the following:

If an unknown number calls and then stops after one or two rings, don’t call it back

Check the number with a Google search to see if it is legitimate or associated with scams. However, be aware that scam numbers are constantly changing, so it may not have garnered any bad reviews at the time you get called

Block it on your phone. Some manufacturers like Apple now flag possible spam calls automatically

Check your phone bill to make sure there are no unexpected international or premium-rate call charges on there

File a complaint with the FCC if you’ve started receiving a high volume of these calls

I’ve already call back: what now?

Don’t panic. Hang up the call immediately. Contact your mobile provider to look for suspicious premium-rate/international call charges and dispute them as fraud. If you handed over any sensitive personal or financial information, contact your bank and tell them what happened. They will be able to advise you how to secure your accounts. If you gave away a password, change it immediately on any site/app you use it.

Phone-based scams are the price we pay for ubiquitous smartphone connectivity. If in doubt, ignore a caller you don’t recognize and check back once they’ve rung off.

FAQ:

What is a wangiri or one-ring phone scam?

When scammers call you and hang up after a ring or two. The aim is usually for them to trick you into calling back and connecting to premium-rate numbers, which generates revenue for them.

Should I call back a missed call from an unknown number?

Never. It may be a scam. If the call is urgent the caller should leave you a voicemail. Always search for the number to see if it is legitimate first.

Can a missed call cost me money?

No. Only if you pick up the phone. It’s always worth looking at your bill though to double check.

Why do I get calls that ring once? Should I call back an international number?

Never call back an international number that you don’t recognize and which has rung only a couple of times before hanging up. It’s likely to be a scam.

What if I called back a one-ring number?

You’ll be connected to a premium-rate (and usually international) number which could cost you a great deal of money.

How do I know if a missed call is a scam?

There are a few red flags. It is an unfamiliar, often international number. It will have rung only once or twice before hanging up. And it may be one of several similar calls coming from different numbers.

Can I be charged just for receiving a one-ring scam call?

Not if you haven’t picked up. However, it’s always worth double-checking with your mobile provider.

Are international missed calls always scams?

No, it could be a legitimate business trying to get in touch with you, like a hotel, or a domestic company with a call center abroad. Still, it’s always best not to answer if you’re unsure and do an online search for the number.

Title: What Business Email Compromise (BEC) Looks Like & How to Catch It
Context: 6% of Identity Threat Detection and Response (ITDR) signals so far in 2026, according to the Huntress Tragic Quadrant, our ranking of the top attacker techniques by impact
Full Text:
If you're looking for a history lesson on your company's finances, start in your inbox, where you might find invoices and vendor details, along with the renewal haggling that shows exactly what you pay and to whom.

Cybercriminals can be history buffs too. Digging through old email threads shows them exactly who to impersonate and how money actually moves. In 2025 alone, the FBI logged more than $20.8 billion in cybercrime losses, with roughly $3 billion tied to business email compromise (BEC), second only to investment fraud.

Business email compromise (BEC) pays because it hides in the long-running vendor and billing conversations you already trust.

"I'd notice if someone was in my inbox"

You might assume you know the signs of an intruder lurking in your mailbox. We've all been trained to recognize the obvious, sloppy signs of phishing.

BEC is stealthier. Often with the help of AI, attackers aim at specific targets by crafting legit-looking phishing and social engineering scams to steal credentials or session tokens for access and persistence. They set up inbox rules that quietly move messages into folders nobody checks, hiding their dirty work in plain sight. This gives them time to figure out how to route money to their own accounts straight from your mailbox.

Here's how that attack chain plays out in a real Microsoft tenant. Huntress CEO Kyle Hanslovan breaks down how attackers sneak into Microsoft 365 mailboxes with low-fi resources to stage attacks like BEC.

What the data says

According to the FBI, reported BEC losses have climbed more than tenfold since 2015.

Figure 1: Reported BEC losses by year. Source: FBI IC3 annual reports, 2015 to 2024.

The Huntress 2026 Cyber Threat Report puts numbers behind the identity tradecraft that fuels BEC:

Logins with a shady footprint made up 37% of the identity threats we tracked, often as the first step toward email compromise and wire fraud.

Adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) attacks, which steal a session token and let the attacker skip the password and the MFA prompt, accounted for 18.9% of identity-based threats in 2025.

Mailbox manipulation and persistence, a key BEC technique, accounts for 24.6% of Identity Threat Detection and Response (ITDR) signals so far in 2026, according to the Huntress Tragic Quadrant, our ranking of the top attacker techniques by impact.

How one gut check stopped a BEC attempt

Latisha Edwards, Accounts Receivable Specialist on the Huntress billing team, received an email that looked like just every other order or renewal message in the queue. It referenced a real partner account with an order form that looked like the right next step.

But something felt off. The order form had a "log in" link embedded in it, which didn't match how this partner usually handled business. Instead of clicking, Latisha emailed her contact at the partner to follow up. That follow-up confirmed the email was a BEC attempt, sent by someone impersonating the partner. Stopping this attack came down to one person slowing down long enough to ask a question. The email looked right because it sat inside a conversation the team already trusted.

Figure 2: A real-world BEC email attempt caught by the Huntress billing team

What you can do to slow down BEC

Now that you've seen what BEC looks like in the wild, let's dig into what you can do about it.

Encouraging your teammates to ask questions is the first step in a good defense against BEC. The Huntress billing team caught this one because Latisha felt safe asking about it.

From there, build good mailbox hygiene habits. The attack can start in your mailbox or arrive as an email from someone posing as a partner, and each one calls for a different kind of check.

For your own mailboxes, watch for inbox rules that don't seem to make sense. Set up alerts for any new forwarding rule, especially one that sends mail to an external domain.

Figure 3: Hidden inbox rules in a 2026 token replay campaign.

For emails that appear to come from partners, flag any request to change account numbers or payment instructions, or any unexpected link that asks you to log in, as high risk, and check the sender's actual address. Verify it directly with your usual contact through a channel you already trust, like a known phone number or portal.

What technology can do to shut down BEC

BEC scams are built to slip right past you. Here's where Huntress fills the gaps.

Managed Identity Threat Detection and Response (ITDR) watches for identity-driven threat behavior across Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace, including session hijacking, suspicious logins, and malicious inbox and forwarding rules, backed by our 24/7 human-led, AI-centric Security Operations Center (SOC).

Managed Identity Security Posture Management (ISPM) works earlier in the attack chain, closing the misconfigurations and policy drift that let attackers into mailboxes and helping enforce conditional access policies.

Managed Security Awareness Training (SAT) helps your people recognize when to pause and verify a change to a payment.

Figure 3: Example of BEC activity flagged by ITDR

The most dangerous BEC email looks exactly like the one you were expecting. Start defending your identities against BEC today with a free trial of Huntress Managed ITDR.

Title: The forced audit: how AuditTeam’s OpsAgent framework masks ransomware as consulting
Context: However, this does not mean the campaign is over, as the latest Rust implants found contained a configuration with the GitHub feature disabled
Full Text:
AuditTeam is an active threat group that uses the OpsAgent framework to compromise organizations across at least seven countries and territories. The campaign began in January 2026 and remained active through October 2026, at a minimum. In its ransom note, AuditTeam demands an “Audit & Consulting fee” in exchange for vulnerability reports. During this period, the group has infected dozens of organizations in Russia, Italy, the Philippines, Hong Kong, Senegal, Finland and China. The group’s leak site also claims victims in seven additional countries.

OpsAgent provides file system management, process injection, privilege escalation, keylogging, screenshot capture, and network pivoting. During the campaign OpsAgent was transitioned from C++ to Rust while adding new capabilities including interactive shells and WebSocket upgrades. Its command-and-control domains use Amazon CloudFront subdomains, which OpsAgent discovers via a public GitHub repository. Two specialized modules extend its functionality. An antivirus/endpoint detection and response (AV/EDR) killer module installs a digitally signed Beijing Jiangmin Antivirus driver to terminate security products. A cryptor module encrypts files using AES-CBC or ChaCha20 with X25519 key exchange and targets database processes for termination prior to doing so.

Background

On March 10, 2026, we discovered suspicious activity targeting an organization in Hong Kong. The tool used was OpsAgent, a framework designed to resemble a penetration testing utility. Further investigation revealed attacks in additional countries, prompting an active research phase. This implant offers extensive operator capabilities, including host reconnaissance, shellcode injection via named pipes, and lateral movement through agent networks based on compromised hosts.

Analysis indicates OpsAgent was used by AuditTeam. The group was first mentioned publicly by dbdigest.com in March 2026. On June 25, 2026, DeXpose reported that AuditTeam had claimed responsibility for an attack on a Russian organization and listed it on its leak site. AuditTeam leaves a ransom note threatening to release stolen data unless a fee is paid. They call this fee the “Audit & Consulting fee.” According to the note, payment results in a vulnerability report being delivered to the victim instead of leaking the stolen data archive to the public internet. While the note does not mention file encryption, it is left by the cryptor module. Therefore, if a victim sees the note, their files are already encrypted.

The ransom note

GitHub commit history shows the campaign started on January 5, 2026. The leak site lists its first victim on February 21, 2026. Dozens of machines across at least seven countries were infected. On August 19, 2026, a C2 domain for the new OpsAgent version was added to the public repository and subsequently used in attacks.

AuditTeam activity timeline

Technical details

Loaders

OpsAgent uses multiple loader variants during its campaign. All discovered loaders unpack OpsAgent by parsing the MZ header and transferring execution to the entry point of the unpacked payload.

The C loader was discovered in April 2026. It injects shellcode into msiexec.exe using standard API calls: CreateProcessA, VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, and CreateRemoteThread.

The .NET loader was found in June 2026. It uses NtQueueApcThread instead of direct process creation for injection. It contains strings such as DApc, DProtect, DResume, and msiexec.exe. Both the C and .NET loaders inject shellcode into a separate target process. They are also protected by OLLVM obfuscation with control-flow flattening enabled.

In September 2026, we discovered the Rust loader. It retrieves an encrypted payload from the C2 server, decrypts it, parses the PE header, and runs the Execute export function within its own process rather than injecting into another process. This in-process execution model eliminates the need for remote process manipulation.

OpsAgent main implant

The implant (version 5.2.8) rivals Cobalt Strike in functionality. It uses a worker-thread architecture: the main thread monitors connection health, while a worker thread processes commands from a queue. Three concepts structure its behavior:

the worker thread (handles nearly all C2 commands)

jobs (background tasks run in separate processes)

links (connections to child agents used for lateral movement)

Exceptions include info, jobs, jobkill, worker_status, worker_restart, and exit, which execute immediately in the main thread.

OpsAgent can optionally obtain its C2 address by reading a public GitHub repository: hxxps://github[.]com/RonaldCMalcolm1983/staticPage. The address is stored in an encrypted form using AES‑CBC with the SHA‑256 hash of f4bb8c7e15d8b98d535eb20b09176b3d as the key and a zero initialization vector. The encrypted payload is wrapped with the markers GetConfig and EndConfig and then base64‑encoded.

Several commands — mimikatz_spawn, execute_assembly, pth_spawn, runpe, monitor start, and screenshot_service start — run background jobs in a separate process. To run a job, each creates a process and a named pipe, and receives shellcode from the C2 server. No command contains embedded mimikatz or PTH binaries. All payloads arrive remotely through the pipe, encrypted with XOR using key 604902af7b70b271. By default these commands use msiexec.exe as a host process, but the path can be changed. The exception is the monitor command, which uses notepad.exe for shellcode injection. This design keeps the implant small and lets operators deliver custom payloads remotely.

Injection commands support two modes: Legacy and DbgInjector. Legacy mode uses CreateProcessA and NtCreateThreadEx. DbgInjector creates a process in DEBUG state, allocates shared memory, sets a hardware breakpoint on FileTimeToSystemTime, then redirects RIP to the shellcode without creating a new thread.

Several code patterns suggest LLM-assisted development. For example, OpsAgent resolves WinAPI functions dynamically by hash: it calculates the hash of a function name, then searches for the matching address. Sometimes the plaintext name remains in memory before hashing. Additionally, all injection commands share near‑identical code structures, differing only in argument count and target process selection. This uniform approach matches LLM‑generated scaffolding.

Commands description

The OpsAgent command set covers file system operations, process management, privilege escalation, shellcode injection, monitoring, and network pivoting. The C2 protocol runs over WebSocket with TLS and exchanges data in units called frames. Protocol frame types function as an extra command set enabling SOCKS proxy establishment, chunked file uploads, and inter-agent data forwarding. These frames are handled by a dedicated frame-handler function rather than the standard command decoder. The following combined table lists all text-based commands and protocol frame types together.

Several commands deserve closer attention. The monitor command manages keylogging through subcommands that start, stop, and configure logging threads. Screenshot features follow a similar design with session management subcommands. In contrast, the pivot subsystem uses a flatter command structure where each pivot command (pivot_list, pivot_start, pivot_stop, pivot_add, pivot_remove, pivot_auto) operates independently without nested subcommand hierarchies.

Some frame type numbers such as 0x20 appear unused in the current implementation. These may be traces of previous versions.

Additional modules

AV/EDR killer module

This module installs a driver disguised as Beijing Jiangmin Antivirus (KV series), utilizing the \KvCorePortX0 filter port for communication. Upon receiving the 0x1D command followed by a target filename, the driver terminates the corresponding process. Its target list covers nearly every major security product on the market.

Additionally, the driver carries a valid digital signature, which facilitates its initial execution.

The process kill list contains approximately 220 entries, including:

Security products: MsMpEng, SecurityHealthService, avp, ekrn, ccSvcHst, fcag, eadrline

Remote access tools: TeamViewer_Desktop, TeamViewer_Service, tv_w32, tv_x64

Monitoring/logging: Sysmon, Sysmon64, splunkd, wazuh-agent

Backup services: VeeamNFSSvc, AcronisAgent, MBAMService

Database processes: sqlservr, mysqld, mongod, redis-server

Cryptor module

This module encrypts files using either AES-CBC or ChaCha20 based on a command-line flag. Each file receives a unique encryption key produced by RtlGenRandom. A 12-byte array serves as the ChaCha20 nonce or expands to a 16-byte AES initialization vector. Key exchange relies on X25519 Diffie-Hellman with a static public key embedded in the binary. The module generates an ephemeral key pair per session and encrypts the file key with ChaCha20 using the shared secret.

Beyond file encryption, the module actively disrupts infrastructure by terminating database processes including SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Redis. It also stops backup services such as Veeam. The module removes shadow copies, empties the recycle bin, and wipes temporary folders. Furthermore, any file deletion overwrites content with random data before removing the entry, preventing forensic recovery.

After encryption, the module drops a ransom note. It formats the message as an audit log demanding payment through a Tor onion address. The note offers two options: pay the “Audit & Consulting fee” for a vulnerability report or face public data disclosure.

Finally, the module’s configuration parameters include file extensions to encrypt, directories and files to whitelist, processes and services to terminate, and shadow copy deletion flags.

OpsAgent-rs (Rust version)

The Rust rewrite maintains functional parity with the C++ version while introducing new capabilities. OpsAgent-rs initially communicates with the C2 via HTTP POST requests to retrieve commands. There are special commands that change this behavior. After receiving an upgrade command, the implant establishes a persistent WebSocket connection over TLS for ongoing C2 communication instead of continuing to send POST requests. Additionally, command identifiers shifted from text names to numeric constants. New commands include interactive shells, directory creation, and sleep-interval changes.

Command mapping between versions shows most legacy commands have Rust equivalents. However, screenshot and monitor commands now consolidate into a unified identifier rather than relying on an extensive set of subcommands. The Rust version removes the entire pivot command set, eliminating pivoting task management functionality.

C2 acquisition in the Rust version changed significantly. The configuration contains a flag controlling whether the implant checks GitHub for new C2 addresses. It also stores markers indicating the beginning and end of the encrypted C2 string. The GitHub README page holds both the legacy C2 format and an additional base64-encoded blob specifically for OpsAgent-rs. The encryption scheme was reworked to use AES-GCM instead of AES-CBC. To derive the GCM key, the decryption flow computes HMAC-SHA256 of the secret key c2-framework-psk-salt-v1 against the configuration data blob, then applies a second HMAC with the salt c2-encryption-key\x01. The nonce is the first 12 bytes of the decrypted payload and the tag occupies the last 16 bytes.

Infrastructure

The implant uses AWS-generated CloudFront CDN subdomains as C2 endpoints. Because these domains operate on shared infrastructure, their underlying IP addresses cannot serve as reliable standalone IOCs.

The GitHub repository stayed active throughout the campaign until November 2026. Commit history shows ongoing updates until September 29, 2026, when the actor deleted the legacy C2 domain from the repository. This suggests the actor maintains the infrastructure actively and rotates domains as needed.

In November 2026, the GitHub repository was removed. However, this does not mean the campaign is over, as the latest Rust implants found contained a configuration with the GitHub feature disabled.

Victims

AuditTeam targets organizations from different countries. We observed victims in China, the Philippines, Senegal, Italy, Finland, Hong Kong and Russia. And according to the group’s leak site, there are victims in Turkey, Thailand, Ukraine, Argentina, South Korea, Japan, and Spain. All identified victims belong to different industries.

Attribution

We attribute the OpsAgent campaign to AuditTeam with high confidence. The following evidence supports this assessment:

Ransom note format and “Audit & Consulting fee” terminology unique to this group

Tor-based leak site listing targeted organizations

Operational philosophy distinguishing them from conventional ransomware groups through remediation reports

Open sources first identified AuditTeam in March 2026 via dbdigest.com. In June, DeXpose reported that AuditTeam claimed responsibility for attacking a Russian organization and listed it on its leak site. The group claims a mission to educate organizations about cybersecurity through exploitation and remediation reports. This tactical approach separates them from traditional ransomware operators.

Conclusions

AuditTeam frames extortion as a paid security audit — a distinctive model among ransomware groups. The C++ to Rust transition signals continued toolchain investment. New Rust commands cover interactive shells, WebSocket upgrades, and directory management.

The specialized modules reveal thorough operational preparation: the AV/EDR killer uses a signed Jiangmin driver to disable security products, and the cryptor module terminates database processes, encrypts files, and removes shadow copies. These tools let the group neutralize defenses and optionally destroy data.

CloudFront CDN subdomains complicate takedown and make IP-based blocking impractical because the IP space is shared with legitimate traffic. While the actor rotates infrastructure, the public GitHub repository enables C2 discovery and its removal disrupts the attack chain.

Custom malware frameworks are typically developed and maintained by APT groups with dedicated engineering resources. AuditTeam shows that a ransomware crew can build comparable tooling. This shift may be enabled by AI-assisted development tools lowering the barrier to creating functional, multi-module implant architectures.

Title: Attackers Compromise Microsoft's Agent Framework PyPI Package to Steal Cloud Credentials
Context: "While directly targeting an official Microsoft package, it seems that attackers found a way to hijack the wheel creation flow to add malicious logic inside
Full Text:
Threat actors have compromised Microsoft's agent-framework package to push a credential stealer, according to reports from Aikido, Chainguard, Endor Labs, OX Security, SafeDep, Socket, StepSecurity, and Google-owned Wiz.

The malicious versions, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were published 33 minutes apart on November 17, 2026, and are designed to run a credential stealer on every Python start. As of writing, both the release versions have been quarantined on the Python Package Index (PyPI) repository. It's unclear how the attacker managed to obtain publishing access.

Agent-framework is the meta-package for Microsoft Agent Framework, an open-source framework for building and orchestrating artificial intelligence (AI) agents using Python.

"Both versions install Python startup hooks that silently collect credentials, environment data, and cloud identity tokens, then exfiltrate them to a webhook[.]site endpoint," Socket said in a report.

Once either of the versions is installed, the package drops a .pth file in the site-packages root directory, which then gets executed automatically on every interpreter start, causing the credential stealer to run whenever Python is started in an environment, even if the package is not explicitly imported.

"Each wheel adds a .pth file to site-packages," Endor Labs said. "Python executes import lines in .pth files on every interpreter start, so the stealer runs on any Python launch in an affected environment, including pip itself, whether or not anything imports Agent Framework."

The names of the .pth files are below -

agent_framework_meta.pth in version 1.26.1

af_runtime_diag.pth in version 1.26.2

The "agent_framework_meta.pth" file contains a single import statement referencing "agent_framework_meta," which then launches the stealer payload. It's capable of capturing the following data -

Environment variables based on substring-based matching

Credential files associated with Azure CLI (~/.azure/*.json), .npmrc, pip.conf, .netrc, .git-credentials, .docker/config.json, Hugging Face, Microsoft Azure DevOps agents, and .env and JSON files

Azure DevOps OIDC tokens

Azure managed-identity tokens

Azure instance metadata and retains up to 8,000 characters of the response

"Besides reading credentials already on disk, the code asks the platform to issue new ones," SafeDep said. "Rotating stored secrets does not cover those."

"In an Azure DevOps pipeline, SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and SYSTEM_OIDCREQUESTURI are enough to request a federated token for api://AzureADTokenExchange. On Azure compute, it asks the managed identity endpoint for an access token to each of these resources. It uses IDENTITY_ENDPOINT or MSI_ENDPOINT on App Service and Functions, and 169.254.169[.]254 elsewhere. It also pulls instance metadata."

It's worth noting that the Azure instance metadata service (IMDS) is a RESTful web service that runs on a local IP address ("169.254.169[.]254"), and provides information about the virtual machine, its region, tags, and the identity token.

All the collected information is saved into a JSON document, zlib-compressed, Base64-encoded, and sent via an HTTPS POST request to a hard-coded URL ("webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb").

Version 1.26.2, on the other hand, imports a new top-level module, af_runtime_diag.py, collects GitHub Actions OIDC tokens, and expands the search patterns used for harvesting credential-related environment variables.

Given that the package attracts about 190,000 downloads a month, users are advised to perform the following steps -

Isolate affected hosts and runners

Pin the package to the most recent safe version (1.26.0) and restore from a clean environment

Check for exposure to the malicious versions between 8:35 and roughly 9:20 p.m. UTC on November 17, 2026

Search proxy and DNS logs for requests to webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb

Rotate exposed credentials from a clean system

Audit Azure identities and review sign-in and activity logs

Audit GitHub Actions workflows that deploy to Azure

"The malicious agent-framework shows how attackers are targeting the AI developer ecosystem and the CI pipelines behind it," OX Security said. "While directly targeting an official Microsoft package, it seems that attackers found a way to hijack the wheel creation flow to add malicious logic inside."

Agent-framework is the second Microsoft-related PyPI package to be compromised this year. In May 2026, the threat actors behind TeamPCP pushed three malicious versions of durabletask, Microsoft's Python client for the Durable Task workflow execution framework, to distribute the Mini Shai-Hulud worm.

Title: Betrayed Expectations: Malware Delivery via Common Brands
Context: By: Jacob Malimban, Intelligence Team In the first half of 2026, Cofense Intelligence observed a 239% rise in phishing campaigns that weaponize brand names to deliver malware...
Full Text:
By: Jacob Malimban, Intelligence Team

In the first half of 2026, Cofense Intelligence observed a 239% rise in phishing campaigns that weaponize brand names to deliver malware onto corporate devices as compared to the first half of 2025. Adobe, the Social Security Administration, Docusign, the IRS, and Zoom are among the most abused. The names are familiar by design: employees who expect a routine document from a recognized sender appear more likely to click, and the borrowed credibility of those brands helps the emails slip past automated security filters. There are two primary ways that brands can be spoofed to deliver malware and abused legitimate remote access tools (RATs).

The first is the initial phishing email. The brand spoofed in the email is what sets the expectation for the context of the campaign. For example, threat actors have used lures such as a refund sent by the IRS (Figure 5) and a benefits-themed document sent by the Social Security Administration (Figure 3). When a victim expects a file but does not realize the sender is malicious, they are likely to click on a phishing link.

The second way a brand can be abused is through the filename. To trick victims, malware may be named “Social_Security_Administration_v02.4_EN_US.msi” (Figure 3) or “setup_Zoom.msi” (Figure 6), depending on the brand used in the phishing email. These malware files are often hosted on cloud services like Google or Amazon, which can bypass the organization’s security controls.

What makes this threat category particularly difficult to manage is that the tools being delivered are not traditional malware. ConnectWise RAT, Datto RMM, SimpleHelp, and similar products are the same software that many IT departments use for legitimate remote support. Threat actors favor them precisely because standard security systems are built to trust them.

Key Points

In the first half of this year, 18% of all malware delivery campaigns impersonated new brands not seen before.

Adobe is the most abused brand when delivering malware in the first half of 2026.

The malware downloaded usually has a filename matching the phishing email branding, like “Adobe software update.msi”.

Threat actors often abuse legitimate cloud services like Google or Amazon to distribute malware and bypass security controls.

94% of campaigns delivering malware abuse legitimate remote access tools (RATs).

Brand Campaign Volume

Malware delivering campaigns increased 239% in the first half of 2026 compared to the first half of 2025.

The top five brands account for around 24% of all malware delivery campaign volume in the first half of this year.

Figure 1: The relative proportion of brands spoofed in the first half of 2026.

In the first half of 2026, Cofense Intelligence identified brands like Adobe, Social Security Administration, Docusign, IRS, and Zoom being abused in malware delivery campaigns. Docusign and Adobe are part of normal organizational operations. These brands follow the trends first identified in 2021. Social Security Administration-spoofing and IRS-spoofing after April mark the trend of government themed phishing outside of the IRS tax season. Zoom has typically been abused to host documents with links to credential phishing pages—and rarely links to malware pages.

Adobe Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware

Adobe-spoofing phishing campaigns rank #1 by volume in the first half of 2026.

Adobe-spoofing phishing emails delivering malware experienced an 18-fold increase when compared to the first half of 2025.

Adobe-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (44%), Datto RMM (16%), and GoTo RAT (7%).

These software are technically legitimate remote access tools (RATs) but can be abused by threat actors to gain unauthorized administrative access.

Figure 2: Adobe-spoofing website claiming a software update is necessary (ATR 415874).

In credential phishing, Adobe has been used to host documents with links to malicious websites. Typically, PDFs with shortened links or QR codes obfuscate the credential phishing pages. In Adobe-spoofing campaigns delivering malware, the email usually claims a document is available to view.

After clicking on the phishing link and attempting to download the document, a website opens. The malicious website typically claims that Adobe Reader is out of date, and an update is necessary to see the PDF. Installing the file will deliver a legitimate RAT controlled by the threat actor. In these Adobe software update phishing campaigns, threat actors like to abuse tools such as ConnectWise’s ScreenConnect (ConnectWise RAT) and Datto RMM to take over the victim machine. For example, Figure 2 shows one website that claims Adobe Reader is out of date and downloads malware. Indicators of compromise (IOCs) for Figure 2 are listed in Active Threat Report (ATR) 415874. ATRs contain the context for each threat actor campaign, allowing current and similar campaigns to be blocked.

Social Security Administration Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware

Social Security Administration-spoofing is the second highest by campaign volume.

Campaign volume in the first half of 2025 is roughly equivalent to volume in the first half of 2026.

SSA-spoofing typically delivers ConnectWise RAT (55%), SimpleHelp (12%), and Faronics Deploy (9%).

Figure 3: Social Security Administration-spoofing email that bypasses email security technology to deliver ConnectWise RAT (ATR 417484).

In the United States, the Social Security Administration (SSA) becomes an important consideration near retirement age (at least age 62). For eligible members of the workforce, this pension information can dictate the lifestyle one lives after employment ends. Previous campaign iterations in Q4 2024 prioritized urgency and consequences when phishing. Current SSA-spoofing emails usually claim to provide information rather than demand it. Figure 3 shows an SSA download statement phishing email, one of the scams the SSA Office of the Inspector General warns about.

If the phishing link is clicked, an SSA-spoofing website typically opens, and a file download starts. The file appears similar to those in the Docusign and Adobe sections. Some files act like benefit letters or document notifications. Others require a download file to be run because “Adobe Reader is out of date”. As usual, running the file will install a threat actor-controlled legitimate RAT. The RATs most commonly installed are ConnectWise RAT and SimpleHelp. The SSA-impersonation campaign delivering ConnectWise RAT has been going on since at least 2024.

Docusign Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware

Docusign-spoofing emails increased about 250% when comparing the first half of 2026 to the first half of 2025.

Docusign-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (34%), GoTo RAT (11%), Itarian RAT (5%), or some combination of the three.

Figure 4: Docusign-spoofing file is a SuperOps RMM instance abused by the threat actor (ATR 415883).

Docusign is typically used by threat actors to host documents with links to redirect to malicious websites, usually Microsoft-spoofing credential phishing pages. This is because using trusted websites help bypass email security technologies, and abusing legitimate business tools helps malicious content mimic benign content. Docusign-branded emails are also useful for getting recipients to download fake documents. Downloading the fake document will deliver malware instead of the expected file.

Threat actors will typically use the Docusign style for the email, the malware download website, and the filename. As seen in Figure 4, a malicious file is named like a Docusign attachment. Threat actors like to deliver legitimate RATs that they control, like ConnectWise RAT and GoTo RAT.

IRS Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware

IRS-spoofing email volume experienced a 10-fold increase when comparing the first half of 2026 to the first half of 2025.

IRS-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (50%), Tiflux RAT (13%), Splashtop (13%) or some combination of the three.

Figure 5: IRS-spoofing, tax refund-themed phishing campaign delivering ConnectWise RAT (ATR 415954).

In the first half of 2025, IRS-spoofing campaigns delivering malware were most prevalent before the USA tax filing date on April 15. Now in the first half of 2026, threat actors continue to use the IRS brand in phishing emails past the tax filing deadline but with many themed about late filing deadlines. Well-developed phishing lures used after April 15 include a refund that has been processed or a tax filing extension being made available. As threat actors use current topics like Elon Musk and DOGE offering an IRS tax refund, IRS-spoofing campaigns are expected to increase.

As with the general rise in threat-actor abused legitimate RATs, IRS-spoofing campaigns deliver similar malware in most cases. ConnectWise RAT is once again the most popular RAT to be abused in IRS-spoofing campaigns. There is also a multi-stage campaign where Tiflux RAT is first installed, then Tiflux RAT installs Splashtop and an UltraVNC utility. In earlier group-delivered malware campaigns, the malware was primarily purpose-built for threat actors and entirely malicious. In the case of Tiflux RAT and Splashtop, both are developed by legitimate organizations for IT operations. Unfortunately, the instances of Tiflux RAT and Splashtop delivered in these campaigns are controlled by threat actors.

Zoom Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware

Zoom-spoofing emails delivering malware increased over 100% when comparing the first half of 2026 to the first half of 2025.

Zoom-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (29%), TrustConnect (14%), and Atera (7%).

Figure 6: A fake Zoom website that downloads an abused RAT (ATR 416603).

Legitimate Zoom links can prompt users to download the Zoom app to access the meeting. Threat actors frequently spoof Zoom and hijack this expected behavior to trick users into downloading malware instead.

Zoom-spoofing phishing emails match the format of legitimate Zoom meeting emails, but the links will redirect to a malware download page instead of the legitimate Zoom site. The most prominent malware delivered is ConnectWise RAT again. TrustConnect and Atera are similar RATs abused by threat actors and delivered in Zoom-spoofing campaigns. Figure 6 shows a malicious Atera instance being downloaded from a threat actor’s website.

Problems Caused by Legitimate Remote Access Tool Abuse

As legitimate RATs are developed for enterprise use, abuse of these tools by threat actors may hide in plain sight.

ConnectWise RAT is currently the most abused legitimate RAT, instead of NetSupport Manager RAT.

When used for their intended purpose, legitimate remote access tools can reduce costs and improve efficiency. With legitimate RATs, IT professionals can easily maintain and monitor various devices across the organization without needing physical access to it. This elevated privilege becomes problematic when threat actors gain access to it.

Legitimate RATs are just as capable of purpose-built malware in the hands of a threat actor. With PowerShell commands, additional malware payloads can be installed after the initial RAT infection. Threat actors have used ConnectWise RAT to deliver ransomware before.

Organizations can find it hard to identify and contain legitimate RATs used by threat actors. Threat actors may even use the same RATs the organization uses, making context, continuous monitoring, and mitigative controls especially important. If the organization successfully contains one type of RAT, threat actors can easily use a different legitimate RAT for infections. In each of the brands spoofed in this report, threat actors already abuse various legitimate RATs.

Conclusions

This report shows five prominent brands spoofed by threat actors. Some key insights include malicious content nearly indistinguishable from legitimate brands, and the increasing abuse of legitimate remote administrative tools. These tactics by the threat actors can make it harder for both users and security analysts to determine if something is legitimate or not. Especially noteworthy are IRS-spoofing and Social Security Administration-spoofing phishing emails. IRS-spoofing emails will likely continue to increase even outside of tax filing season. Social Security Administration-spoofing emails already are not limited by a specific season.

Page Break

Mitigations

Establish and enforce a software allowlist for remote access tools. Any remote access tool not on that list, including ConnectWise, SimpleHelp, Atera, and GoTo RAT, should be blocked from installing on corporate devices. Organizations that do not have an allowlist should at minimum block the digital certificates associated with remote access tools they do not use.

Update employee security awareness training to reflect current lure themes, specifically Adobe document requests, SSA benefit notices, IRS refund emails, and Zoom meeting invitations. Employees who have been trained on real, current threats are more likely to pause before clicking. Simulation exercises should use these exact scenarios, not outdated generic examples.

Blocking remote access tools and updating training are essential, but threat actors will keep finding new brands, filenames, and legitimate tools to abuse. Organizations need a way to respond quickly when a campaign reaches the inbox or an endpoint. Title: The Next Cyberattack Won’t Wait. Are You Ready?
Context: On November 17, CISA urged organizations to patch a critical Oracle Java vulnerability
Full Text:
One day into the November Microsoft outage, Cofense Intelligence saw phishing emails posing as service notifications. The outage was real. The emails were designed to steal sign-in credentials. We published our findings on November 16. On November 17, CISA urged organizations to patch a critical Oracle Java vulnerability. Security teams should act on the patch guidance and keep email defenses running while they address it.

Read our November 16 Flash Alert · Read CISA’s November 17 alert

One campaign can look like many

The FBI has warned that criminals use generative AI to make scams more convincing and easier to scale. In polymorphic phishing, different versions of the same campaign can land in different inboxes. AI can help attackers produce more of those variants. Even modern filters can miss a message that’s been designed to evade AI algorithms.

For a security team, the work starts when the first report comes in. Removing that one message protects the person who reported it. Finding the other versions can protect employees who received a similar email and haven’t flagged it. That’s why teams need a way to investigate across inboxes.

Why AI alone isn’t enough

AI is essential to modern security. It processes volume and speed that no team could match by hand. But AI struggles with threats that don’t match previous patterns, and new lures are exactly what attackers are producing. Human analysts close that gap. They judge intent and context, and they respond to what automation hasn’t learned yet. Reports from employees and customers feed back into protection, so one organization’s report can help protect many others.

In one recent case, a brand-new lure got past several automated systems, including AI-based ones. Employees at a Cofense Phishing Defense Center customer reported the lure, in turn giving Cofense analysts the opportunity to protect all of our customers from this threat. Speed and human judgment working together made the difference. Cofense has seen a 22% growth from 2025 to 2026 so far in non-Microsoft related branding being used in phishing attacks as AI allows Threat Actors to expand upon the types of threats they are able to create. Depending on the industry, between 39% and 49% of phishing subject lines included the recipient’s name or other personal details. It is becoming increasingly easy for threat actors to use AI to harvest employee information and use it in phishing campaigns.

Find the campaign and remove it

Say one employee reports a fake service alert. Start with that email, then check whether other inboxes received related versions. AI helps group similar messages for analyst review. An analyst confirms which emails are malicious so the team can remove them, including copies nobody reported. That’s the difference between closing one report and removing the campaign.

See how Cofense Vision AI connects related messages

What organizations can do now

Walk through the steps below with the people who own email security, IT, and incident response. Start by checking who can remove a confirmed phish from multiple inboxes and how your team will coordinate if email is down.

Have Cyber Security solutions that are able to be flexible in the everchanging landscape of cybercrime and AI. You should have human resources working in tandem with supervised AI to ensure that you aren't left waiting for AI security models to catch up.

Map out alternative communication strategies for when you lose access to email or messaging platforms.

Have and verify backups for all important company data.

Ensure your internal Phishing Training programs are properly training your employees based on real life threats and targets weaknesses in your user base.

Document clear lines of communication. Employees should know who to contact when verifying a request or transaction. They should also know which backup channels to use if they suspect the original source has been compromised.

Don’t rely on a single layer of defense. No filter catches everything and attackers design campaigns to bypass them. Pair your automated security tools with detection and response to ensure that someone is finding what is slipping through.

Treat legitimate remote access tools with the utmost scrutiny. Attackers often abuse legitimate remote monitoring and remote management (RMM) tools, such as ConnectWise/ScreenConnect, because those tools blend in with normal IT activity. Block any RMM or remote access software your organization doesn't officially use and closely monitor the ones you do.

Patch with vetted updates. Apply tested patches for every known vulnerability. Prioritize anything actively exploited or facing the internet, like VPNs, firewalls, and remote access appliances.

Shrink your attack surface. Review and remove old or unused accounts, services, appliances, and applications. Anything you don't need is just one more way in.

Flag external email clearly. Use clear banners to warn users when a message comes from outside the organization. That simple visual cue helps users spot business email compromise (BEC) and impersonation attempts.

Title: Russian COLD RELIC Hackers Use Stolen Google Workspace Data to Breach Second U.S. Organization
Context: Attacks mounted by the threat actor have successfully compromised high-value targets, including government officials, defense contractors, and non-governmental organizations...
Full Text:
The Russia-linked cyber espionage group known as Cold Relic (formerly COLDRIVER and UNC4057) has been observed weaponizing a single cloud compromise into a launchpad for a series of linked intrusions resulting in third-party compromise.

Google's Mandiant and Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said it investigated a 2026 compromise at a U.S.-based organization in which the adversary leveraged data, the corporate staff directory, and identities harvested from an earlier attack on another U.S.-based entity in late 2025.

Cold Relic, also tracked as Callisto, Gossamer Bear, and Star Blizzard, has a track record of orchestrating sophisticated phishing and malware campaigns to gain access information that may be of strategic importance to the Russian government.

The access is abused to register rogue multi-factor authentication (MFA) devices, passkeys, and MFA backup codes to establish long-term persistence and then conduct aggressive data collection and exfiltration operations targeting email, chat, and cloud storage repositories. In addition, the compromised access is used to target the victim's social and professional networks.

Attacks mounted by the threat actor have successfully compromised high-value targets, including government officials, defense contractors, and non-governmental organizations (NGOs) across Europe and North America.

"Once Cold Relic compromises a target, it uses stolen emails and data to establish authentic pretexts and impersonate contacts when reaching out to subsequent targets," Google said.

According to the tech giant's cybersecurity and incident response teams, Cold Relic compromised the cloud productivity environment of an unspecified U.S.-based organization in late 2025. Initial access to the network was achieved by means of a residential proxy network located in close geographical proximity to the victim.

Using the stolen credentials of a Super Admin account and combining it with an MFA push notification fatigue attack, the threat actor is said to have gained access to the account after the victim accepted an MFA request. This was followed by the attacker registering their own device within the tenant to retain access. The threat actor was also observed using passkeys and MFA backup codes as alternate access mechanisms.

"Cold Relic used the privileges of the compromised Super Admin account to download the contents of the entire organization's cloud storage drive by both mass sharing files to a Cold Relic-operated email account and downloading files directly," Google explained.

"While operating inside the tenant of the victim organization, Cold Relic accessed the Admin Console, queried Admin security investigation and email audit logs to check defensive visibility, and viewed, modified, and deleted Alert Center notifications to remove forensic evidence of the initial intrusion."

These actions ultimately enabled the threat actor to export full employee lists and domain-wide data via the Google Takeout service using the Super Admin privileges. Following mass data theft, the attackers continued to maintain access over several months and perform additional activities -

Sync email inbox via OAuth to external email clients.

Re-authenticate using unrevoked attacker-enrolled passkeys that persisted across password and session resets and bypassed device registration controls.

Target cloud drive document access related to credentials, email archives, personnel information, and other documents of interest.

Even after the attackers were ousted from the victim organization, Google said it observed Cold Relic using email accounts impersonating employees of the victim organization to target both internal employees and associates within the same professional circles as part of a renewed social engineering campaign.

The attack then moved to the next phase when the threat actor compromised a Microsoft Entra ID user account of a second U.S.-based organization that used Entra ID as its federated single sign-on (SSO) identity provider for Google Workspace.

By impersonating an employee at the first organization, the threat actor established communications with the target over a secure messaging app and then shared phishing links designed to harvest credentials and authentication tokens for Entra ID under the pretext of sharing a document containing details about a technical issue.

"Upon successful authentication using the stolen credentials, Cold Relic registered and used a new MFA device in the SSO solution to retain access to the user account throughout the intrusion," Google said.

"By impersonating someone known in the same professional circles as the new target, Cold Relic increased their chance of phishing success. Ultimately, in this case, Cold Relic was able to obtain credentials to the organization and perform bulk download of files accessible in the compromised user's cloud drive."

Upon successfully compromising the second organization, the messaging app account used to initiate the conversation had its profile name changed to a different persona. It's suspected that the new persona was likely used to target other organizations in the same professional network.

"Cold Relic's campaigns demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse," Google said. "By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners."
