Title: Uncovering GhostMap: The Rootkit Behind Shai-Hulud’s Rusty Cousin
Context: Watching only the installer’s child processes would therefore have missed the actual loader
Full Text:
How does IronWorm install and load GhostMap?

GhostMap runs as part of a larger implant. IronWorm handles installation, service persistence and collection; the rootkit provides concealment and anti-debugging. The sequence below follows the tested npm specimen from installation into those kernel mechanisms. It does not represent a complete infection followed through external command and control.

Figure 1. Two delivery channels with a shared execution pattern. In the compared payloads, installation creates a persistent service. The service loads the GhostMap rootkit component and operates the local collector. The detailed measurements below come from the IronWorm specimen.

Stage 1: IronWorm establishes persistence and loads GhostMap

JFrog documented a preinstall entry that invokes ./tools/setup during installation of [email protected] when lifecycle scripts are enabled. In the AUR channel, modified PKGBUILDs install atomic-lockfile, whose install hook executes its bundled Linux binary.

The npm page for [email protected] was marked as deprecated with the author message: “COMPROMISED via Mini Shai-Hulud worm (TeamPCP). Upgrade to latest.” This is the package author’s attribution in the warning; our analysis does not independently establish who developed or operated IronWorm. The screenshot documents deprecation, not removal from the registry.

Figure 2. Historical npm page screenshot showing the deprecation warning for [email protected] and its reference to Mini Shai-Hulud (TeamPCP).

Our runtime investigation began with the extracted executable, run with root privileges in the lab. In the initial runtime investigation, the specimen copied itself to /var/lib/glugi/glugi, created glugi.service and enabled the service. The executable started by systemd had the same hash as the original sample.

That successor process loaded GhostMap’s eBPF components. Watching only the installer’s child processes would therefore have missed the actual loader. Names varied across runs. One later installation used /var/lib/havebi/havebi. These paths are observed examples, not fixed names that every infection must use.

Stage 2: GhostMap attaches its eBPF programs to kernel events eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) lets small programs run at defined points inside the Linux kernel. A program holds the logic; a hook is where it runs, such as a syscall exit. A link represents the attachment. A map stores data that programs consult or update, and a helper is a kernel function they can call under applicable restrictions.

GhostMap comprised 13 programs, 10 maps and 13 links at an active checkpoint in the IronWorm run. For process hiding, hidden_names holds selected process names. An execution hook can add matching processes to hidden_pids. Another map, scratch, temporarily records the address of a directory result buffer. For socket hiding, hidden_inodes stores socket inode identifiers, which the network concealment programs use to select entries.

Figure 3. Reconstructed terminal view of saved bpftool JSON, filtered for readability. On November 8, hidden_names selected dbus-daemon, hidden_pids held five PIDs and hidden_inodes held inode 23875. Memory evidence linked that inode to the listener on port 8738. Map IDs belong to this run.

Stage 3: GhostMap changes the answer delivered to the reader Linux exposes process information through /proc, a virtual filesystem. Its numeric directory names are process IDs (PIDs). The ps utility lists processes by reading this information.

A syscall is a request from an application to the kernel. The getdents64 syscall returns directory entries in a buffer in application memory. Each record contains a name and a length field, d_reclen, which tells the reader how far to advance to the next record.

GhostMap’s enter_getdents program remembers the buffer address. At sys_exit_getdents64, its exit_getdents program examines the returned records and checks numeric names against hidden_pids. When it finds a selected entry, it uses bpf_probe_write_user to modify the record chain. Increasing the preceding record’s length makes the reader advance past the hidden entry.

The saved map dumps make the selection concrete. We named benign test processes dbus-daemon to exercise the name matching. In the November 8 experiment, hidden_pids included benign test processes 3035 and 3934. Both disappeared from /proc enumeration while their known /proc/PID paths remained accessible. Control processes 3031 and 3930 were absent from the hiding map and remained listed. After the rootkit stopped, the hidden test processes became visible again.

Figure 4. Terminal reconstruction of a comparison computed from the same November 8 snapshots. Benign test PIDs 3035 and 3934 are in hidden_pids and missing from enumeration, but remain directly accessible and return after stopping the rootkit. Control PIDs 3031 and 3930 remain visible.

Hiding is not automatically inherited from a parent. A fork creates a child process; an exec loads a new program into a process. GhostMap’s on_exec hook checks the process’s short kernel name, comm, against hidden_names and adds a matching PID to hidden_pids. In our November 12 test, a fork-only child remained visible even though it inherited the name dbus-daemon. A child that executed a program with that name became hidden, even under a visible parent. A visible child with a parent missing from ps is therefore a useful hunting lead, but not proof of rootkit activity on its own.

Stage 4: One changed byte makes the reader skip a record In a separate experiment on November 10, we captured each directory buffer before GhostMap’s syscall exit hook and compared it with the same buffer delivered to a controlled reader. Matching the thread, buffer address and syscall interval let us identify precisely what changed.

In a controlled directory, the preceding record’s length changed from 32 to 56 bytes. The reader consequently skipped a file whose numeric name matched the hidden process’s PID. In /proc, a record length changed from 24 to 72 bytes, skipping the malware process and the hidden test process.

Each case reproduced three times. Across all six altered buffers, only one byte changed: the low byte of the two byte length field. The hidden records’ bytes remained in the buffer, and the syscall’s returned byte count stayed unchanged.

Figure 5. Terminal reconstruction displaying saved buffer measurements: the preceding record grows from 24 to 72 bytes, causing the reader to skip two PID entries.

The comparison stayed byte identical across 24 calls made before the rootkit started or after it stopped. Actual ps queries also omitted the hidden test process, both with and without our observer running. After the rootkit stopped, ps displayed the process again.

Figure 6. Reconstructed, filtered ps output from the November 10 experiment. While the rootkit is active, only control PID 3821 appears. After it stops, target PID 3820 appears too. The recorded command was ps -eo pid=; filtering was added for presentation. These PIDs belong to a separate run from Figures 3 and 4.

Stage 5: Socket concealment changes two different views Linux exposes socket information through more than one interface. /proc/net/tcp provides a text listing, while socket diagnostic requests over Netlink return structured messages that tools such as ss can interpret. GhostMap targets both paths.

In a separate listener experiment, GhostMap’s hidden_inodes map contained inode 18544, identifying IronWorm’s listener on 127.0.0.1:8738. This is a different run from Figure 3, where that listener had inode 23875; inode numbers are local to the observed socket instance. The listener disappeared from /proc/net/tcp in all three observations, while a benign listener on port 8739 remained visible.

The Netlink path produced a different result. GhostMap changed the listener’s diagnostic message type to NLMSG_NOOP, indicating a no-operation message, but left its port, identifier and listening state in the payload. The tested ss utility still displayed the listener in all three queries, although its process-owner annotation was absent. The corresponding upstream source provides a plausible explanation: its parsing path can read the retained payload without requiring the original message type.

The concealment code ran, but it did not hide the socket from that reader. The result applies to the tested ss package, iproute2 6.1.0-1ubuntu6.4; other consumers may handle the modified message differently.

Figure 7. Terminal reconstruction of the separate listener experiment: port 8738 is absent from /proc/net/tcp but visible to the tested ss utility; control port 8739 is visible in both. The hidden inode in this run was 18544, not the 23875 shown in Figure 3.

Title: “Amazon” job offer promises $5,000 a month, but it’s got all the signs of a scam
Context: Available with Malwarebytes Premium Security for all your devices, and in the Malwarebytes app for iOS and Android
Full Text:
Last month, Amazon announced plans to hire more than 300,000 people in the US for the holidays. That’s welcome news for job seekers, but scammers know that.

We found several sites advertising a remote assistant job under Amazon-like names, with promises of up to $5,000 a month. None of the sites is run by Amazon.

Amazon says all genuine job opportunities are posted on amazon.jobs; hourly warehouse jobs are also listed at hiring.amazon.com. The offers we found are separate from Amazon’s holiday hiring push.

The application doesn’t match the job description

One careers page calls the role a “legitimate, fully remote position,” with “no commute, no office, no fixed desk.” Yet the form asks whether applicants have reliable access to a personal vehicle and someone at home who can receive packages. Those questions point to package handling, not remote assistant work.

A recruitment page promises fully remote work paying up to $5,000 a month

Why Amazon makes such good bait

People expect Amazon to be hiring. A hiring announcement can make an “Amazon is hiring” message seem plausible. But the remote assistant jobs on these sites are separate from Amazon’s announced seasonal roles.

“Working with Amazon” can sound believable. Businesses can provide services to Amazon sellers without being part of Amazon. The sites use names that resemble those of logistics or seller-support businesses, which can make the connection harder to judge at a glance.

The pitch targets people looking for flexible work. “Work from home” and a few hours a day can appeal to parents, students, and people looking for a second job.

The tactic has been used before. Amazon says it saw more reports of scammers posing as recruiters in September and October 2025. In June, we warned about Amazon job texts offering $250 to $500 a day for 60 to 90 minutes of work. The sites we found add a careers site, a company website, and a polished application form to make the offer look more convincing.

Several names, apparent links

We found multiple recruitment and application sites using Amazon-like branding:

amzssapplication[.]com and jobsamzss[.]com, two careers pages for the “Remote Assistant” job

applyamazonsp[.]com, an application form for the same job, under the name “Amazon Seller Pro LLC”

The sites use byte-identical site icons. Their domains were registered through the same registrar between July 23 and October 26. These similarities suggest a connection, although they do not establish who operates each site.

The same remote assistant pitch appears on another domain

The recruitment pages list “HR” email addresses on three additional domains: amzncrew[.]com, joinamzn[.]com, and workatamzn[.]com. These addresses do not establish an affiliation with Amazon.

To verify a job with Amazon itself, check its official job boards at amazon.jobs or hiring.amazon.com. Independent businesses serving Amazon sellers hire separately, so verify their offers by contacting the business through contact details you find independently.

The recruitment pages link to amzshippings[.]com, a website advertising preparation and shipping services for Amazon sellers. That’s a newly registered domain with hidden ownership details.

A remote job that asks about your car and doorstep

Although the careers pages on these sites describe the role as fully remote, the application asks:

“Do you have reliable access to a personal vehicle?” If not, it asks applicants to explain how they would transport packages.

“If you’re not home, is there a person to receive parcels?”

A remote assistant wouldn’t normally need to receive or transport packages. These questions are warning signs of reshipping, also known as parcel-mule fraud.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) says that a job asking you to receive shipments, repackage them, and send them elsewhere is a reshipping scam. The goods may have been bought with stolen payment details, and people recruited this way can be left handling packages connected to fraud.

The form collects personal information

The application form asks applicants for personal information

The form collects your name, phone, email, home address including apartment number, felony history, education and employment history. It promises “Your data is secure” and sends submissions through Formspree, a third-party form service. We could not establish who receives the information. The page also tells search engines not to index it.

No resume is needed. Instead, the careers page says: “Our HR team calls you directly … Keep your phone on — we don’t schedule in advance.“

In the page code, that note sits below a leftover template comment: “PASTE YOUR TEXT HERE.”

The recruitment page’s footer states: “Amazon Shipping Services is not affiliated with or endorsed by Amazon.com, Inc.”

What could happen if you apply?

Sharing your details could expose you to identity theft. If you take the job, you could also be asked to move packages or money tied to fraud.

Identity theft: Your name, contact details, and home address can be useful to criminals. Be especially cautious if anyone later asks for your Social Security number, bank details, or ID.

Being drawn into fraud: If you receive or forward packages bought with stolen payment details, your address may be linked to their movement.

Losing money: A fake employer might later send a check and ask you to return some of the money or use it to buy supplies. The FTC warns that fake checks can bounce after the money has been sent on.

How to stay safe

Find Amazon jobs on amazon.jobs. Amazon says genuine job opportunities are listed on its official job board.

Check the domain, not the logo. Anyone can copy Amazon’s colors and branding.

Be wary of high pay for little work, especially when there’s no résumé or scheduled interview.

Don’t receive or forward packages for an employer you haven’t verified.

Don’t send ID photos, your Social Security number, or money before verifying the employer.

If you already applied, don’t give an unscheduled caller your bank details, ID, or money. If you shared sensitive information, follow the steps at IdentityTheft.gov and consider placing a credit freeze.

How Malwarebytes helps

Malwarebytes Browser Guard blocks scam pages like these. And if you’re not sure whether a job offer is real, give the link or put a screenshot of the offer into Malwarebytes Scam Guard before you reply. It will assess whether it’s a scam and give you advice on what to do next.

Title: Microsoft Warns of Coordinated Phishing Campaign Leveraging M365 Service Outage
Context: “This is consistent with historical attacker campaigns which continuously look for notable global events to exploit in their social engineering lures,” Microsoft wrote in a blog...
Full Text:
Microsoft has identified a “coordinated, high volume” global phishing campaign designed to exploit the recent Microsoft 365 outage.

The campaign was observed on November 13, as the company grappled with rolling out a fix for the tech failure impacting services like Outlook and Teams worldwide.

The outage began on 11.20 EST on November 12 and lasted over 22 hours, with Microsoft confirming that its services were fully restored on 23.15 EST on November 13.

The phishing emails were designed to exploit individuals’ and employees’ desperation to reconnect to M365 services, attempting to entice them into clicking a malicious link and capturing their credentials.

The messages impersonated legitimate M365 service-health notifications. They aimed to create a false sense of urgency by claiming that the recipient’s emails had been held during a service disruption and would be deleted within 24 hours unless the recipient took action to restore them.

“This is consistent with historical attacker campaigns which continuously look for notable global events to exploit in their social engineering lures,” Microsoft wrote in a blog dated November 16.

There is currently no evidence of credential capture, malware delivery or post-compromise activity emanating from the campaign. However, organizations have been urged to investigate whether any users clicked the malicious links and take immediate steps to mitigate any malicious activity if this did occur.

How the Phishing Campaign Unfolded

The email lures sent during the campaign used the subject pattern “Outage – <random token>” and display names built from a three-character, organization-style prefix followed by “Outage Notification” or “Service Health.”

Microsoft said the use of specific sender domain names, such as moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com and newbooker[.]com, were designed to make the messages more tailored and appear relevant to the recipient.

The messages commonly used 24-hour deletion deadlines and call to actions using prominent “RESTORE MESSAGES” links to drive immediate action. They also referenced Microsoft services like Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and Copilot.

The body of the messages included fake email conversations positioned to be hidden from the recipient, which appears to be an attempt at mail filtering evasion.

In this article

Attackers used Optimizely to spread code targeting visitors’ payments and devices

Researchers found affected files linked to 178 organizations, including CNN, BBC, and Zoom

If you visited an affected site on November 16, check your payments and update your devices

Visiting a familiar website should not mean exposing your payment details to criminals. But attackers found a way to put malicious code on websites belonging to some of the world’s best-known organizations by compromising a service those sites trusted.

On November 16, security researcher Scott Helme and his team at Report URI identified malicious JavaScript in Optimizely files associated with 178 organizations, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom, Salesforce, and GitLab. The code could redirect cryptocurrency payments, skim payment card details, and deliver exploit kits targeting vulnerable iPhones and iPads. Check Report URI’s full list to see which websites were affected.

Optimizely provides software that helps businesses test and personalize their websites. To accomplish this, a website adds a small piece of JavaScript called a snippet. This loads Optimizely’s code into visitors’ browsers, where it can change their experience and measure the results. In this incident, it also provided a way for unauthorized changes to reach visitors through an otherwise legitimate website.

Optimizely is widely used. Website technology tracker BuiltWith currently reports detecting it on roughly 190,000 live websites. That is its overall usage, not the number affected by this incident. This qualifies as a supply-chain attack because, instead of breaking into every website separately, criminals abused a shared service those websites relied on.

The BBC provides a prominent example of how the attack unfolded. Report URI’s timeline records a clean capture of its Optimizely snippet at 02:21 UTC on November 16, followed by an injected version at 04:21 UTC. By 08:28 UTC, the researchers observed the main malicious payload being loaded on bbc.com.

This does not establish that the BBC’s own servers were breached, or that every BBC visitor was infected. It shows how a third-party script used by a trusted website can become the route through which malicious code reaches a visitor’s browser.

Optimizely confirmed the incident and says it fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects. Report URI also said all the infected Optimizely files it was monitoring were clean by 23:11 UTC on November 16 and had remained clean since.

How to stay safe

Visitors cannot reasonably be expected to inspect every script a website loads, and disabling JavaScript can make many websites unusable. The most useful steps are to keep devices updated and check any potentially affected transactions.

Update your iPhone or iPad. Install the latest iOS or iPadOS version available for your device. This is particularly important if you visited an affected website on November 16, because the attack included exploit delivery aimed at older, vulnerable versions.

Use an up-to-date real-time anti-malware solution. This can help detect and block malware on your devices.

Review cryptocurrency transfers made during the incident. Check the actual destination address against the intended recipient’s address, confirming it directly with the recipient through a trusted channel. The attack was specifically designed to change payment destinations.

Check payment card activity. If you entered card details on an affected page on November 16, monitor your account and contact your card issuer promptly about suspicious transactions. Enable transaction alerts where available. You could also consider identity theft protection with credit monitoring to help spot signs of identity misuse, such as new credit accounts opened in your name.

Watch for unusual account activity. Investigate unexpected account changes or unfamiliar sessions, particularly for services you were using on affected pages. The code could steal some cookies, which can contain information used to keep you signed in.

The main responsibility rests with the organizations delivering code to visitors. The incident shows why website operators also need to monitor what third-party scripts do and restrict the other scripts and data connections they can introduce. Consumers shouldn’t have to audit a website’s software supply chain before reading the news or making a purchase.

Title: Hackers Found a Way Around GitHub SHA Pinning. This Webinar Explains How to Close the Gap
Context: Attackers have already found a way around it
Full Text:
Pinning GitHub Actions to an exact version of their code, known as SHA pinning, has become the go-to defense against software supply chain attacks. Attackers have already found a way around it.

In March 2026, the hackers who hijacked Trivy, a widely used open-source security scanner, planted malicious code that looked like it came from GitHub's official checkout tool. They even labeled it a security fix. Teams pinned to it would have passed every check.

The trick works because GitHub lets copies of a project, called forks, share code with the original. In May, the same technique hit the popular actions-cool/issues-helper tool, stealing credentials from the pipelines that ran it.

The lesson: pinning guarantees the code won't change, but not who wrote it.

That gap is the focus of an upcoming webinar, GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning. If your team treats pinning as the finish line, save your seat to learn what it actually protects you from, and what it doesn't.

Immutability Is Not Provenance

Pinning earned its reputation. When the tj-actions/changed-files compromise repointed tags to a malicious commit across more than 23,000 repositories in March 2025, teams that had pinned to SHAs were unaffected.

GitHub now lets administrators enforce pinning as an organization-wide policy, and few security teams argue against it.

📅 Save Your Spot: Learn Why “Best Practice” Won’t Stop the Next GitHub Actions Attack

But a pinned SHA leaves three questions unanswered:

Authorship: A SHA doesn't tell you who wrote the commit. Any fork commit can be pinned.

Project membership: Org-level enforcement checks that a reference is a 40-character SHA, not that the commit actually lives in the upstream project.

Runtime: A Docker-based action pinned to a SHA can still build its image at runtime, pulling in dependencies that were never frozen.

With agentic development pushing more code through CI than ever, each of those gaps gets exercised more often and reviewed less closely.

GitHub's Lockfiles Help. They Don't Finish the Job.

GitHub's 2026 Actions security roadmap, published March 26, put deterministic dependency locking front and center. Workflow lockfiles entered public preview on October 14 and became generally available on October 28, 2026. They tie every run to recorded commits for actions and their transitive dependencies, even if a tag moves later.

That's real progress. Locked commits must exist on a branch of the source repository, which blunts fork-only impostors. But GitHub's own changelog is clear that locking "does not determine whether the dependency itself is safe." Commit authorship and runtime builds remain open; immutable releases only help when maintainers opt in, and lockfiles aren't currently supported on GitHub Enterprise Server.

Not sure where your pipelines fall in that gap? Register for the webinar for a clear-eyed breakdown of what GitHub's roadmap fixes and what it still leaves to you.

What You'll Learn

Led by Erika Heidi, Staff Developer Relations Engineer at Chainguard, the session draws a hard line between immutability and provenance, and covers:

What org-level pin enforcement actually verifies, and the false confidence it can create

How impostor commits work, and why GitHub's repository network makes them possible

What GitHub's Actions roadmap addresses, and what it doesn't

Other ways to close the trust gap, including a curated catalog of vetted actions

Who Should Attend

Platform and DevOps engineers who own CI/CD, AppSec and DevSecOps teams writing pipeline policy, and security leaders who signed off on SHA pinning as "done." If your workflows pull in third-party actions, this session is for you.

Attackers have already shown they can disguise a malicious commit as a hardening fix. The next one won't announce itself either.

Register now for GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning, pick the session time that works for you, and find out what your pins aren't telling you.

Title: Opinion pollster Ipsos 'fesses up to 'cybersecurity incident'
Context: In a statement issued on Monday from its Paris headquarters, the company confirmed it filed a complaint over the attack on November 11, but gave few details because its internal...
Full Text: Market research giant Ipsos says it's currently investigating a "cybersecurity incident," and has reported the matter to the authorities. In a statement issued on Monday from its Paris headquarters, the company confirmed it filed a complaint over the attack on November 11, but gave few details because its internal investigation is ongoing. "Upon discovery, we promptly activated our incident response procedures, took steps to contain the incident, and engaged external cybersecurity specialists to support our investigation," it said [PDF]. "The investigation is ongoing to determine the nature and scope of the incident. We have reported the matter to the relevant authorities." Ipsos confirmed the attack had no impact on its operations or customer service delivery, however, it did not comment on the nature of the attack or whether any data was compromised. "We take protection of the information entrusted to us very seriously," Ipsos added. "Should the investigation establish that information relating to clients, projects or business partners has been affected, we will contact those concerned directly. "As the investigation is ongoing, we are not in a position to comment further at this stage." The company declined our requests for additional data, as it does not want to release unverified information to the market. Founded in France in 1975, Ipsos is one of the leading market research companies in the world, employing nearly 20,000 people and operating in 220 cities across 90 markets. It is routinely engaged by businesses for its market research data, as well as by public sector organizations for its opinion polling, often responsible for providing data regarding political views and satisfaction surveys. Tasked with procuring a wealth of data on myriad topics, Ipsos also offers data analytics services that turn the information it gathers through research, polls, and surveys into insights that inform organizations' business strategies. ®

Title: Facebook may have access to your entire photo gallery
Context: Meta announced an opt-in photo suggestions feature for the US and Canada in October 2025
Full Text:

In this article

Facebook’s photo suggestions feature could access your entire gallery through a single permission

Italy fined Meta €805 million and says the privacy violation remains ongoing for some users

Check Facebook’s photo permissions to control what it can access

If you’ve given Facebook access to your phone’s photos, the app may be able to read your entire gallery, including pictures you never intended to share. Check your photo permissions if you want to limit that access.

Italy’s data protection authority, the Garante, has fined Meta €805 million (about $887 million) for accessing Android users’ entire camera rolls without specific consent or adequate disclosure. The regulator says the violation remains ongoing for some users, despite changes Meta has made.

The decision concerns Facebook’s “Get camera roll suggestions when you’re browsing Facebook” feature. Launched in 2023, the idea is to use your photos and videos to suggest potential social media posts.

You might be surprised to hear that Facebook can access every photo or video in your gallery if you’ve granted full photo access. That includes pictures of your kids, restaurant receipts, and that Wi-Fi password label you photographed awkwardly on the router behind the TV. But you might have granted that access without realizing it also enabled photo suggestions. That’s the problem, said the regulator.

Facebook’s app requested access to the camera roll through a single permission that applies across the entire app, covering multiple features with different requirements. The Garante said:

“The permission is preceded by a non-specific notice (’enable other features’) which does not make it clear to the user that they are also authorising suggestions from the camera roll.”

One permission, lots of features

Asking permission for lots of things via one request violated Article 122 of the Italian Data Protection Code, according to the regulator. That code is Italy’s privacy law, and its Article 122 implements the EU’s ePrivacy Directive, which protects data stored on devices such as smartphones. The Garante said access for this feature required free and informed consent.

Facebook also failed to adequately explain its use of the photo gallery, and the suggestions feature was on by default. Granting full photo access could give the app ongoing access to the entire library, the regulator said, without users being able to verify which information was actually being used.

The regulator’s investigation started in July 2025 after consumer organization Centro Tutela Consumatori Utenti submitted a report. That prompted the Garante to conduct its own technical analysis.

Meta had asked for Ireland to handle the case. Like many other technology companies, Meta’s main EU presence is in Ireland, whose regulator handles many cross-border privacy cases. The Garante rejected that argument because the ePrivacy rules at issue do not use that system.

Meta disagrees

Meta told Reuters that users must grant device permission before the feature can operate and can change that permission in their settings.

The social media company also called the fine, which amounts to less than 0.5% of global revenues, “disproportionate.” It will appeal, it told reporters.

The Garante attributed the amount of the fine to the high number of people affected (around 20 million Android users in Italy) along with the duration of the incident, which it referred to as a breach. It also called Meta out for its “poor level of cooperation.” Changes that the company made to its app were introduced late and only applied to users who update the app, it added.

Aside from the financial penalty, the regulator has ordered Meta to request consent separately for the camera roll suggestions feature. It must get that consent after explaining to users what it will use the data for and how to disable it. The company must turn it off by default even for those who previously gave the blanket permission, it said, and if it doesn’t comply by the 60-day deadline then it must not enable the feature for users who haven’t given consent.

The regulator is preparing for a potential follow-up. It has left the door open to address the possible use of content to train AI, which Meta has denied. The Garante also “reserves the right” to assess a new feature that allows the content of the camera roll to be processed in the cloud.

Meta announced an opt-in photo suggestions feature for the US and Canada in October 2025. It analyzes media to find memorable moments and suggests creative edits. Meta says suggestions remain private unless users choose to share them, and the feature can be turned off in Facebook’s camera roll settings.

What Facebook users can do

The Italian order does not automatically change permissions for users elsewhere, but you can review your own settings.

On Android, go to Settings > Apps > Facebook > Permissions > Photos and videos, then select Don’t allow to revoke gallery access. Depending on your Android version and the app, you may also have an option to allow access only to selected photos and videos. Menu names can vary by device.

While Italy’s decision didn’t target iPhone users, they can also review Facebook’s photo access under Settings > Privacy & Security > Photos.

Mobile protection, anywhere, anytime.

Title: Holiday shopping in a world of fakes: How AI is changing the game
Context: *Malwarebytes threat intelligence data, collected between 1 November 2025 and 31 October 2026 Scammers are getting personal Nearly one in four consumers (24%) say they’ve...
Full Text:
It’s the most wonderful time of the year, especially for scammers.

The holiday shopping season is packed with tempting one-day-only deals, gift guides, and retailers promising the perfect present at the perfect price.

And wherever shoppers go, scammers aren’t far behind.

Cybercriminals have always taken advantage of the holiday rush. Now AI makes it easier to create fake storefronts, products, reviews, and promotions that look and sound legitimate. For consumers, knowing what—and who—to trust is getting harder.

Shoppers are worried. According to Malwarebytes research, 77% of consumers are concerned about being scammed by a retailer using a fake AI website, or using AI to misrepresent products or reviews.

That concern is grounded in experience: More than one in four consumers (28%) have experienced an AI-related shopping scam in the past year Some were misled by AI-generated product photos or reviews. Others described ordering products that never arrived, sometimes from legitimate-looking websites that turned out to be fake.

With the holiday shopping season upon us, we’re looking at how AI is changing the shopping experience, where consumers see risks and benefits, and how to shop more safely.

When a great looking product isn’t what it seems

Realistic product images, glowing reviews, and professional-looking websites can make unfamiliar retailers seem trustworthy. AI makes it easier to create all three in one polished package, which is convincing enough to deceive even careful shoppers.

For some, these convincing fakes have made buying online feel unsettling. One survey respondent commented:

“It seems as though when I’m shopping online, I notice the models are AI-generated or even the products themselves and that scares me. I can’t tell what’s real or not anymore. I don’t even know if what I’m looking to buy is real! I don’t know if what is being advertised is the actual product. AI is going too far.”

Survey respondents shared real-life experiences that help explain those fears. One described receiving products that looked nothing like the photos:

“I buy fewer items that I don’t already know from real life because I fell for manipulated images and the delivered items barely resembled the edited pictures in the shop!”

This aligns with what we’re seeing too. As an example, earlier this year we found cat face flower seeds being sold online.

But manipulated images don’t have to look this extreme, or this obvious. As AI improves, telling what’s genuine from what’s fake is getting much more difficult.

Some of our survey respondents described seeing convincing fake storefronts that took their money without delivering anything:

“It was a fake website promoting shoes. I bought them and it turned out to be an AI website. Now I’ll be more wary of these websites and what they look like.”

These experiences are especially common among younger shoppers. 42% of Gen Z say they’ve experienced an AI-related shopping scam, compared with 30% of Millennials, 22% of Gen X, and just 9% of Boomers and older.

The impact goes beyond lost money or a missing package. Respondents described feeling embarrassed, angry and unsettled by how convincing the deception was. For many, that experience left a lasting distrust of online retailers.

How AI brings scams directly to shoppers

Scammers don’t have to wait for shoppers to stumble across a fake website. With the help of AI, they can send convincing, personalized messages that appear to come from familiar brands, bringing scams directly to consumers.

It’s no wonder that global mega-retailer Amazon is the most impersonated brand that we see in our threat intelligence data, followed by Walmart, Temu, Costco, and Steam.

*Malwarebytes threat intelligence data, collected between 1 November 2025 and 31 October 2026

Scammers are getting personal

Nearly one in four consumers (24%) say they’ve received a scam message that felt highly personalised, sometimes including their name or other personal details. Among Gen Z, that figure rises to almost one in three (32%).

We came across a scam that linked a person’s phone number and name with a fake Facebook Marketplace listing to act as a conversation lure and get them to respond. Answering a message is often the first step in what can become a very costly scam.

Even when shoppers spot the warning signs, a personalised scam can leave them feeling uneasy. One respondent explained:

“I received an email that was clearly directed to me personally, yet it seemed “off” which was an alarm for me. I investigated it before clicking on anything and knew then that it was a scam. It made me feel like nothing is safe out there anymore and you have to be hyper-alert at every moment when online.”

Spotting scams among the shopping noise

Delivery companies are an obvious choice for scammers to impersonate at this time of year. With more purchases being made, it can be hard to keep track of which retailer is using which delivery service, and on which date it will arrive.

*Malwarebytes threat intelligence data, collected between 1 November 2025 and 31 October 2026

Common delivery scam lures we’ve seen include:

A delayed parcel notification, paired with a request to pay a small fee through a link

A failed-delivery claim demanding address confirmation or rescheduling.

Short deadlines or “final notice” language to create a sense of urgency.

Lookalike delivery company domains and off-brand links.

In this example, scammers use a fake missed delivery, the USPS brand, and a sense of urgency (48 hours) in order to get their target to click.

The broader research shows just how challenging this environment has become:

85% agree that sophisticated scams can be hard to distinguish from the real thing

85% believe AI makes it easier for scammers and criminals to target people

Even the most routine messages about purchases and deliveries warrant a closer look, and that’s one more thing for consumers to worry about during an already busy time of year.

Where shoppers accept AI

Despite their concerns, many consumers accept some uses of AI in retail. In the survey, 43% say it’s okay for businesses to use AI-generated websites to sell products, while 36% accept AI-generated salespeople. Including neutral responses, those figures rise to 72% and 64%, respectively.

There’s also growing acceptance of AI on the retailer side. 43% say it’s okay for businesses to use AI-generated websites to sell products, while 36% are okay with AI-generated salespeople. Including those who feel neutral about these practices, the figures rise to 72% and 64%, respectively. That shows how willing consumers are to let AI into the shopping process, despite their concerns.

That acceptance extends to product images: 60% say using AI to enhance them is no different from existing advertising practices. Product photos have long been staged, edited and polished to make merchandise look its best; AI can do the same.

Shoppers’ responses show that concern about AI and acceptance of its use can coexist. In the holiday rush, distinguishing a useful shopping aid from a convincing deception can be difficult.

Shoppers are taking precautions, but the burden is growing

Some shoppers are responding in practical ways, starting with where they choose to buy:

36% have limited purchases from unfamiliar online retailers.

26% have limited purchases from social media accounts

As one respondent explained:

“I am more wary of purchasing something from an ad I see on social media. I tend to search for the item online myself and find a legit website to order from.”

Others are checking information more carefully:

One respondent described checking reviews on another website after watching a convincing product video on social media, only to uncover signs of a scam. Another now deliberately seeks out negative or neutral reviews and real customer photos. Others describe comparing information across multiple sources rather than taking any online content at face value.

One respondent summed up the need for extra caution:

“I tell my children not everything that glitters is gold. Always be careful and check everything yourself. With AI today you can make everything look beautiful but beautiful doesn’t mean true, correct or authentic. Fact checking is the order of the day.”

Beyond checking information for themselves, consumers also value having another person to turn to when they need help. Nearly seven in ten (69%) say they’d spend extra time or pay more for human customer service, while 43% say they’ve tried to talk to a real person rather than an AI customer service system.

AI may make shopping more convenient for some, but that doesn’t mean consumers want to rely on it for every interaction.

How to spot AI-powered shopping scams this holiday season

AI can make fake stores, product photos, and reviews look extremely convincing. Here are four ways to protect yourself:

Slow down. Scammers use urgency to rush you. During the holidays, limited-time deals and delivery alerts can be especially persuasive. Don’t let a countdown or unexpected message stop you from checking first.

Guard your information. Be wary of unexpected requests from sellers or delivery services for passwords, payment details, or other personal information. A message can use your name or mention a recent purchase and still be fake. You can check which data

Verify the source. Check independent reviews and compare product photos and details across websites. Go to the retailer’s official site directly instead of following links in messages. Remember that logos, email addresses, and caller IDs can all be faked.

Use anti-scam/scam detection tools. Malwarebytes offers free tools to help you spot and stop potential scams. If you’re worried about the legitimacy of a DM, text, email, link, or number, upload it to Scam Guard. We’ll give you a verdict on whether it’s safe, along with guidance on what to do next. You can also use Browser Guard as you shop to block scammy and fraudulent websites, and stop card skimmers in their tracks.

About the research

The research in this article is based on a March 2026 survey about AI, identity, and digital trust, conducted among 1,500 respondents in the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. The research was prepared by an independent research consultant and distributed via Forsta.

Title: New GitDoor and GraphDoor Backdoors Turn GitHub and SharePoint Into Covert C2 Channels

Full Text:
Government sectors in Asia and Africa have been targeted by an active cyber intrusion campaign that delivers to previously undocumented backdoors that leverage legitimate services like Microsoft SharePoint and GitHub for command‑and‑control (C2).

The activity has been codenamed Operation ShadowCloud by Kaspersky. The Russian cybersecurity company said it identified the campaign in early 2026.

"The threat actor behind it is abusing the legitimate MeshAgent utility to drop two brand-new backdoors," Kaspersky researchers Saurabh Sharma and Noushin Shabab said in a two-part analysis. "These implants hide their command‑and‑control (C2) traffic behind cloud services Microsoft SharePoint, GitHub, and Ably, allowing the implants to blend in with normal traffic, effectively evading network-based detections."

The modular backdoors, dubbed GraphDoor and GitDoor for their choice of the cloud platform used for C2, enable the download of additional plugins on demand and the execution of shellcode directly in memory to extend their functionality. Traffic between infected systems and the C2 servers is proxied by deploying a modified Erfrp client and Ably messaging service-based plugins.

The starting point of the attack has been traced back to a MeshCentral Agent, a legitimate remote access tool that's used for remote desktop control, command‑line access, and file management. The attack is said to have targeted an unspecified Taiwanese organization.

The exact method by which the utility is installed on the host remains unknown. However, signs point to the "reuse of a prior infection already present on the network," Kaspersky added.

The MeshCentral Agent is configured to contact a hard-coded C2 server ("wss://27.102.66[.]162:443/agent.ashx") and then fetch three payloads staged on the endpoint -

A legitimate binary used for DLL sideloading (start.exe, pythonw.exe, and zoomit.exe)

A rogue loader DLL used to unpack and execute the next-stage malware (jli.dll, SbieDll.dll, python39.dll, WINMM.dll, and libcef.dll)

An encrypted file containing the core payload

At least two different DLL loaders have been identified to date, each employing its own method to decode and launch the encrypted backdoor payload by injecting it into the current process's memory.

"Loader (Type 1) employs a hybrid scheme: first running the data through an RC4 stream cipher and then applying an XOR mask, while Loader (Type 2) simplifies the process by using a straight XOR operation alone," Kaspersky noted.

The end goal is to deploy backdoors like GitDoor and GraphDoor, which employ a number of encryption and obfuscation techniques like control flow flattening and nested helper functions to complicate analysis efforts and make it harder to trace genuine execution flow.

GitDoor, as the name implies, uses GitHub for C2. It relies on two distinct repositories for receiving command payloads ("/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Havo") and uploading the results of the execution ("/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Trix"). While the Havo repository is public, the Trix repository is private.

The creation date of these repositories suggests that preparations for the campaign have been underway since at least the end of 2024. GitDoor supports 26 commands that allow the backdoor to -

Perform file management

Log keystrokes

Launch a proxy, including using Ably

Load shellcode to Base64-encoded Common Object File Format (COFF) binaries and terminate the backdoor

The custom shellcode feature is used to download and run different modules that facilitate the following functions -

Conduct process injection using methods like Asynchronous Procedure Call (APC) injection

Enumerate and manage Windows services

List files and directories, wipe file contents, and recursively delete a directory

Conduct network-related activity by displaying active TCP connections and modify firewall rules

Manage processes, including dumping the memory of the process with a specified process ID into a file and terminating specific processes

Execute commands using "cmd.exe"

Enumerate, create, and run scheduled tasks

Enumeration Windows Registry keys and values recursively and set a value in the Registry

Extract user information, along with local groups and its members

Add of a new Windows user account or add a user to a global or a local group

Record keystrokes to a file ("%APPDATA%\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\Cache\logs.dat")

Dump cookies from Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge directly from the process memory using CookieKatz

Use Mimikatz to dump credentials from Windows LSASS

Capture screenshots of the entire screen or a specific window identified by its process ID

Extract WhatsApp's database decryption key

Initiate NTLM authentication to an attacker-controlled destination

Calculate system idle time and display the last time a user was active on the host using mouse movement and keyboard input

GraphDoor, on the other hand, opens a named pipe, creates a directory named "Intel_Log" inside the system's Application Data folder, and gathers system information to send back to the attacker.

To establish communications with the C2 server, it authenticates with a malicious application using "login.microsoftonline.com" on port 443 and uses the access token to communicate with the Microsoft Graph API and ultimately stage the data on the SharePoint drive.

The malware then fetches three plugin modules from the server and launches them in parallel to carry out screenshot capture, process listing, and keylogging. It also proceeds to reestablish contact with the SharePoint website to retrieve the commands to be executed on the machine.

The complete list of plugins supported by GraphDoor is as follows -

kl.ts, to log keystrokes at "%APPDATA%\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\Cache\logs.dat"

pr.ts, to list running processes

scr.ts, to take screenshots of the window that matches a supplied process ID and save them as JPEG images

moveDir.ts, to move the legitimate executable, the malicious loader DLL, and the encrypted backdoor file to specific target path

channel.ts, to launch the proxy

abchannel.ts, to use the Ably messaging service to proxy traffic

ab2channel.ts, a covert SOCKS5 proxy that tunnels TCP traffic through Ably's Pusher‑compatible WebSocket service

In addition, GraphDoor's custom shellcode capability expands on GitDoor to support two additional commands that allow it to run commands using "cmd.exe," as well as MZ executables.

The identity of the threat actor behind the campaign is unknown, but Kaspersky said it shares some degree of overlap with a China-nexus activity that Sophos tracks under the moniker Bronze Sandcastle. Tactical similarities have been observed with prior campaigns undertaken by FamousSparrow and CopperTurtle (aka BlackTech).

"On several victim systems, these groups shared the same staging directories as the GitDoor backdoor, with their implants deployed within a one-day window of GitDoor deployment," the company concluded. "While this does not prove a direct link, it suggests that a Chinese-speaking group may be developing and/or utilizing the GitDoor and GraphDoor backdoors."

"By using cloud-based storage and messaging services, the actors blend in with normal traffic (as cloud API calls to Microsoft Graph, GitHub, and Ably are indistinguishable from legitimate enterprise usage, evading many network-based detections), and enable dynamic payload delivery, where on-demand plug-ins and shellcode are retrieved from cloud repositories, allowing for rapid updates and functional extensions without modifying host files."

Title: Attackers Pick the Target, AI Does the Rest: Cyber Predictions for 2027
Context: We expect more of the same in 2027: encrypting ransomware as the steady baseline, with extortion-only waves arriving whenever an attacker finds a zero-day in widely used software
Full Text:
Key points

Humans will pick the target, but AI will run most of the attack.

AI credentials will become the new cloud keys.

Shadow AI agents will present a new challenge.

Patching alone will not be enough to tackle modern threats.

Ransomware will break another record, with data-theft waves on top.

The line between spies and criminals will keep blurring.

As the AI juggernaut continues to roll on, in 2027 we may reach a point where cyber attackers need to do little more than pick a target and collect the money, information or access at the end. AI agents will increasingly handle reconnaissance, exploitation, credential theft and lateral movement, working at machine pace.

Last year, we predicted that agentic AI would lower the barrier to entry for attackers. Over the past 12 months we have watched that happen, and most of our predictions for 2027 extend what we are already seeing, while one or two go further. As organizations give AI agents standing access to their data, we would not be surprised to see a major breach in which the attacker brought almost no tools of their own, because the victim’s own agents did the work.

Humans will pick the target, but AI will run most of the attack

Until recently, attackers used AI as an assistant, however, increasingly, they are putting it in charge. The “Skynet” agent we reported on in October 2026 wired a large language model (LLM) into the center of an attack tool. The tool had around 74 callable functions covering reconnaissance, exploitation, credential theft and botnet control. Its operators described the unattended setting as “Skynet mode” and authorized it to run up to 100,000 steps without human approval.

This is not yet the norm. Most intrusions still have a human at the keyboard making the important decisions. But the direction is clear, and Google’s threat analysts and others have described the same shift from chat-based assistance to agentic orchestration. An agent does not sleep, does not need to be paid and can run many intrusions at once. An operator who once handled one victim at a time could now supervise agents’ activity on dozens.

While agents deployed in most organizations today still run under constrained scopes or human-in-the-loop approvals, they are vulnerable to prompt injection attacks or indirect tool abuse, which could place them under the control of attackers without them even needing to exploit a vulnerability to send the agent rogue. Prompt injection attacks involve the hackers feeding a malicious prompt directly into a LLM that they have gained access to, while an indirect attack involves hackers hiding their payloads or instructions in data consumed by the LLM – such as software tickets, code reviews or web pages that the LLM has been instructed to read. The attackers are essentially tricking the LLM, no vulnerabilities required.

Model poisoning is another way that attackers can potentially interfere with AI agents’ operations. It involves tampering with the data, fine-tuning samples, or open-source weights that an AI uses to learn, so that the AI develops a deliberate blind spot or backdoor known only to the attacker. Security teams are generally so worried about protecting credentials and endpoints, they may not think about whether the intelligence inside the model itself has been compromised. These attacks are also often difficult to detect as the model appears to be functioning normally, and strange outputs may simply be put down to hallucinations.

In 2027 and beyond we expect the human role in many AI-driven cyber attacks to shrink towards choosing targets and collecting the money. Reconnaissance, exploitation, credential theft and lateral movement will increasingly be handled by agents working at machine pace, which means the gap between first access and damage will keep closing. Low-skilled attackers will benefit most: capabilities that once needed a team of specialists will be available to anyone who can point an agent at a list of targets. For defenders, the quality of attacker tradecraft will matter less than its volume.

Agents will also change what attackers use. Living off the land, where attackers use tools already present on the victim’s network, has been one of the defining tactics of the past decade. The next version may be living off the AI: attackers turning the victim’s own coding assistants and agents, and the permissions they hold, against the organization. Gartner forecast task-specific agents in around 40% of enterprise applications by the end of this year, and every one of them holds standing credentials and access to data. We would not be surprised to see the first major breach in which the attacker brought almost no tooling of their own, because the victim’s agents did the work.

AI credentials will become the new cloud keys

Attackers learned long ago that cloud credentials were worth stealing, and AI credentials are their newest target. Our recent research on the Aoki infostealer found it harvesting credential and session files for Claude, Codex, Cursor, Gemini and other AI coding assistants. Skynet, for its part, scans for exposed AI endpoints and uses them to fund and conceal its operations, leaving the victim to pay for every step.

There is a market for what they steal. Google found that underground prices for AI accounts more than doubled in 2026. Stolen AI access is useful in several ways: free computing power, a way around bans imposed on accounts that have been abused, and a way to strip safety controls from commercial models. Attackers can steal AI access in order to run AI-driven attacks.

In 2027, we expect AI keys to join browser cookies and crypto wallets as a standard target for infostealers, and for the resale of stolen AI access to mature into its own underground business, much as initial access brokers did for network access. Developers will be the main targets. A coding assistant’s configuration files can tie together API keys, source code repositories and cloud accounts, which makes a developer’s workstation one of the most valuable machines in the organization. Many victims will discover the theft through an unexpected bill, not an alert.

AI providers will respond with shorter-lived tokens and tighter controls, as the cloud providers did. Attackers will respond by stealing live sessions instead of static keys. If the history of cloud credentials is a guide, it will take organizations a couple of painful years to treat AI credentials with the same care as the rest.

Shadow AI agents will present a new challenge

As the use of AI continues to become more commonplace across almost all organizations and workplaces, we may see a shift from the traditional issue of “shadow IT” where software, hardware, or other services are used without the knowledge or approval of the enterprise’s IT department, to “agent shadow IT”, where AI tools are being used without the knowledge or approval of organizations’ IT or security departments.

This could be employees using things like AI tools, local models, or unapproved plugins to get their work done faster, without telling their IT or security departments. This is likely to become a bigger issue and has been observed already today where security teams cannot protect what they do not know exists. These unofficial AI helpers often have direct access to company data and code, which may get fed back to whoever is running the AI without restrictions or specialized agreements being in place instructing the AI not to leverage or use the data, leading to this becoming a leak or information disclosure issue.

This could also be a more pronounced issue in markets where the popular, Western AI coding assistants are not legitimately available, leading to those wanting to use them turning to rogue operators. A recent Symantec Threat Hunter Team blog discussed how a grey market relay service was installing the genuine OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code CLIs on enterprise systems and then reconfiguring them to route every request through third-party infrastructure instead of the vendors' own servers. This activity was mostly impacting a variety of enterprises across mainland China where many Western AI coding assistants are not officially available.

Of note was that this operation also disabled the CLI's execution sandbox entirely, enabling network access for the write sandbox, replacing the user's real API credentials with relay-issued tokens, and disabling telemetry and error reporting. While there was no evidence found in this case that the relay operator had abused their level of access, a potential risk is that the configuration it installed would let the operator read every prompt, file, and secret passed through the agent and run commands with the user's full privileges. Given this was not a legitimate service, it’s unlikely any IT or security oversight for this product existed in the organizations where it was being used.

Patching alone will not be enough to tackle modern threats

The PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) show how short the patching window has become. Both flaws allow unauthenticated remote code execution. Technical details leaked on October 20, 2026, a day before the PHP project released fixes, and public proof-of-concept code followed. Attackers did not need to be clever. They just needed to be early.

Defenders are told to patch faster, but patching is a race against machines that defenders cannot win. Testing and deploying a critical patch takes days or weeks, and for some systems, like those older PHP versions, it never happens. AI is shrinking the patching window. It can increasingly read a patch, compare it with the old code and produce a working exploit in minutes, and it can scan open-source projects for flaws before the fixes ship.

Vulnerabilities are also only part of the problem. Attackers using AI are just as good at finding what has no CVE: misconfigurations, forgotten internet-facing systems, default or reused credentials and over-permissioned identities, and at chaining several low-severity weaknesses into a working attack path. In 2027 we expect more breaches in which no single vulnerability was to blame.

So, we expect the conversation to shift from how fast organizations patch to how fast they can make a threat irrelevant, whether or not a patch exists. Think of it as mean time to mitigate. The answer will lean on controls that do not depend on knowing the vulnerability: behavioral blocking, default-deny application control, tight segmentation and identity protections that stop an attacker using what they have stolen. Patching will still matter. It just may not be enough.

Ransomware will break another record, with data-theft waves on top

Ransomware shows no sign of slowing. There were 3,126 claimed attacks in the third quarter of 2026, the highest quarterly total we have recorded, including the busiest single month, August, with 1,184. Across the first three quarters of 2026 there were 7,777 claimed attacks, 28% more than in the same period of 2025 and already close to the 8,498 recorded in the whole of last year.

The line-up behind those numbers keeps changing. Over the past 12 months, Qilin has been the busiest operation with 1,457 claimed attacks, followed by The Gentlemen with 870, a group that did not feature in our 2025 top 10. Akira (604), Inc (482) and DragonForce (391) follow behind. LockBit, which had struggled to rebuild after the disruption of its operation in 2024, is back with 365.

Data-theft-only extortion is less predictable. It surged in 2025, driven by a handful of mass campaigns, notably Cl0p’s attacks on Oracle E-Business Suite and the Salesforce-related attacks carried out by ShinyHunters, and it fell back in 2026, with 808 identified extortion-only attacks in the first three-quarters of 2026, against 1,187 a year earlier. One campaign against a vulnerability in a widely used enterprise product can add hundreds of victims of these kinds of attacks in a single quarter, making the likely volume of these kinds of attacks harder to predict.

We expect more of the same in 2027: encrypting ransomware as the steady baseline, with extortion-only waves arriving whenever an attacker finds a zero-day in widely used software. Encryption may keep its place partly because it pays better: Coveware found victims paid in only around 15% of cases in the second quarter of 2026 where leaking data was the only threat.

The line between spies and criminals will keep blurring

Many of the threat actors we track no longer fit neatly into a single category. Our research on Jewelbug found a China-based group running espionage operations and a cryptocurrency fraud business from the same infrastructure and the same control panel. On one side it compromised government webmail in the Middle East. On the other, it ran an AI-generated network of fake exchange download pages to target Chinese-speaking crypto users. We assess that the fraud business most likely supplied access, infrastructure and delivery for the espionage.

Warlock, a ransomware operation we wrote about in our Ransomware 2026 whitepaper and blogged about more recently in October 2026, fits the pattern too. Some of its tools trace back to earlier Chinese espionage activity, and ransomware may at times serve to obscure espionage.

We expect this to go further in 2027. Governments that want deniable capabilities have every incentive to let contractors fund themselves through e-crime, and criminals gain tooling, protection or simply tolerance in return. The result is groups whose motives change from one intrusion to the next: espionage on Monday, extortion on Friday.

We expect to see more high-profile incidents in which ransomware turns out to have been a cover for espionage or sabotage, and incident responders will have to start asking what the ransomware was hiding. Attribution will get harder, and the stakes will rise with it. Defenders may need to stop running separate playbooks for ransomware and espionage. Every ransomware incident should include a search for earlier access and for what was taken before anything was encrypted.

What to do about it?

Several of the trends above share one answer: reduce what attackers can do once they are on a network. Behavioral protection, visibility across endpoints and cloud, and governing how AI is used inside your organization matter more than ever when exploits arrive faster than patches. For resource-strapped teams or complex enterprises looking to deepen visibility and correlate signals across their stack, solutions such as Symantec CBX can fill that gap.

Title: A phishing page interested in MX records, (Tue, Nov 17th)
Context: Of course, MX records are publicly available, and there is nothing preventing an attacker from looking them up independently
Full Text:
I’ve mentioned before in some of my diaries that it can be instructive to look at what appear to be “generic” phishing messages in detail from time to time, since some of them might prove not to be as generic as they initially appear. I came across a good example of this while going over phishing messages delivered to our handler inbox over the past few weeks, when a message that, at first glance, appeared to be a fairly ordinary attempt at stealing e-mail credentials turned out to lead to a page interested in collecting a little more information than just the victim's password.

As you can see, the original message was not especially noteworthy on its own, being a spin on the usual “your password will expire today” approach…

The link pointed to an HTML page hosted on Google Cloud Storage, with the recipient's e-mail address included in the URL fragment:

hxxps[:]//storage[.]googleapis[.]com/alx2/03/1a/we.html#[recipient_e-mail_address]

After opening the link, the recipient would be presented with a generic login form, personalized using the domain part of their e-mail address. The page also attempted to use a screenshot of the legitimate website of the recipient's organization as its background, which it retrieved using the thum.io service. This didn't work quite as intended for isc.sans.edu, since the screenshot service returned an error message instead of the requested image. However, when I modified the URL to contain an e-mail address from another domain, the resulting page looked considerably more convincing.

Looking at the source code revealed a couple of layers of URL-encoding and additional JavaScript obfuscation. Once these were removed, the page turned out to contain a fairly typical credential-harvesting kit, which supported multiple languages and attempted to collect not just the submitted password, but also the visitor's public IP address, geographic location, browser information and language. This information, along with a timestamp, was supposed to be sent to the attacker using the Telegram Bot API.

Such extensive collection of information is not particularly unusual. In fact, another phishing page that I examined recently collected a similarly extensive set of information and also sent it to the attacker using Telegram. In the present case, however, one additional field included in the information sent to the attacker caught my attention – it was labeled "MX Record".

A closer look at the corresponding code revealed that the JavaScript actually performed a DNS-over-HTTPS query for MX records associated with the victim's e-mail domain, using Google's public DNS service. The relevant parts of the code (slightly simplified and reformatted for readability) looked as follows:

... const response = await fetch( "https://dns.google/resolve?name=" + domain + "&type=MX" ); const data = await response.json(); return data.Answer.map(answer => answer.data).join("\n"); ...

The retrieved records were then included in the message containing the stolen credentials:

... message += "MX Record : " + await getMXRecord(domain) + "\n"; ...

The use of MX records in phishing is certainly not new. For example, Infoblox documented a phishing-as-a-service operation called Morphing Meerkat in March 2025, which used DNS-over-HTTPS queries for MX records to identify victims' e-mail service providers and dynamically select appropriate phishing templates[1].

In the present case, however, the MX records weren't used to customize the phishing page. Instead, the lookup was performed as part of the credential collection process, and its results were included in the information sent to the attacker.

Of course, MX records are publicly available, and there is nothing preventing an attacker from looking them up independently. Nevertheless, including them with each set of stolen credentials would help the attacker automatically identify the e-mail infrastructure used by the targeted organization, which could be useful for further attacks or for prioritizing the collected credentials.

Whether the threat actor behind this particular phishing actually used the collected MX records in this (or any) way is impossible to say. Still, having the phishing page perform a little additional reconnaissance on the victim's organization, and including the results with the stolen credentials, seems like a noteworthy detail in an otherwise fairly ordinary phishing kit…

[1] https://www.infoblox.com/blog/threat-intelligence/a-phishing-tale-of-doh-and-dns-mx-abuse/

----------- Jan Kopriva LinkedIn Nettles Consulting
